speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our manpower policies must adjust dynamically to such structural changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Singapore workforce and the manpower policy system that supports the workforce are core national assets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without our world-class workforce, companies would not invest more and there would be no continued creation of good jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a critical pillar to Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Businesses and investors, both local and overseas, watch our manpower policies closely for the same reason.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It requires years of building, innovating and fine-tuning this system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is inherently complex, balancing sometimes diametrically opposite intentions and expectations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, we need to strengthen our Singaporean Core, but not lose access to talent needed for Singapore to be competitive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to create good work opportunities for our locals without starving businesses of the manpower to grow and survive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must grow our economic pie but not weaken our compact with workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will speak on structural changes from COVID-19 and how we need to respond to survive and thrive in the new world order while navigating difficult policy tensions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Digital and technological changes driven by COVID-19 have created many jobs, but also destroyed many others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can no longer take sustained full-time employment for granted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers are likely to not stay in full-time or traditional employment for as long as before.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry continue to safeguard the retirement adequacy of our workers amidst such structural changes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers might not be accumulating CPF savings consistently or there might be disruptions to building up their retirement nest when they do gig or contract work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is tempting to ask for flexibility in withdrawals to make up for lost income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But this comes at the expense of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The complexity deepens with a volatile investment climate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With increasing investment uncertainty, how can the CPF Board still ensure good returns for our workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There has also been a pervasive shift towards greater focus on skills rather than jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was precipitated by a global marketplace where skills rather than occupations or academic qualifications reap ever higher economic rent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, how do we employ artificial intelligence (AI) in our work pass system to identify skills and bring in foreign manpower that creates better value for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, for employers, it is more relevant and intuitive to hire based on skills rather than job titles or school qualifications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the default is still rather traditional, relying on the presumed hiring certainty of job titles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry help businesses to develop a new dimension in hiring and rewarding for skills?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has stretched on long enough for workers to re-examine their careers, working conditions, reward system and purpose.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was particularly stark amongst the younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many were as concerned about their work prospects as they are about wellness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The perhaps already archaic 5Cs that were once deemed as the Singaporean dream is now overtaken by other non-traditional aggregators of success, such as work-life balance and purposeful careers, aligned to their passions and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has far-reaching consequences for the workforce and workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the importance of wellness as a capability within the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over the years, there are decreasing numbers of jobs that pose physical harm and safety worries as Singapore develops into a service and higher technology economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, mental stress hits all of us, regardless of industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Globally, companies have introduced well-being programmes in the wake of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These programmes help employees with mental health and physical health.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The improvements in personal outcomes have a direct impact on productivity and retention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Wellness goes beyond just providing yoga classes during lunchtime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In Sweden, there is a concept of fika.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It roughly means drinking coffee, eating sweet or savoury pastries and chatting with co-workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is even a sequence to doing fika.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One starts with cinnamon buns and ends with a princess cake.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Swedes see this as an essential part of managing work stress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is not to say that mandating fika or, in our context, "kopi breaks" is that panacea to our workplace issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a bigger cultural and work construct to it and fika is possibly that symbolic reminder of the need for work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The takeaway is that we can no longer treat employee mental wellness as just another good-to-have if we want to deal with changing workplace demands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, the bliss or curse of the hybrid workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some workers like it, others detest it but nearly all can see the value of working from home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 forced most companies to have their workers to work from home but few have well-developed hybrid workplace policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, work time and place become increasingly and agonisingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Where it was the flexible work arrangement that workers have been craving for years, it is now a bane, especially for younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The solution is also not to bring all workers back to the office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers have experienced the savings from commuting and employers do save from office rental.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to a 2021 CNBC/SurveyMonkey Workforce Survey, nearly 80% of workers want to work for a company that values diversity, equity and inclusion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This might not fully reflect the situation in Singapore but there is clearly a greater desire amongst younger workers for similar aims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers increasingly want their companies to take a position on such matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a clear signal that Singapore does not tolerate discrimination in workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This move underpins a whole-of-nation desire for greater inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the law provides for minimal standards, we need to push the front end of the charge for greater inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to look into establishing public indices, so that companies can benchmark their progress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can provide for broader and faster progress on the important issue of inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, going green is no longer a tagline but a real driver of change in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The green economy will be a key driver in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have the Green Plan 2030 to advance our pursuit of sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must now prepare our workers to make the transition into the green economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some jobs in the petrochemical sector might, indeed, be lost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proliferation of remote working has shrunk the global workplace into one global connected office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Physical presence at the workplace is not tied to productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During the deepest of COVID-19, many companies have started sourcing services from overseas for work that used to be done here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Remote working has allowed them to capitalise on global talent pools while saving costs and even rental costs of office spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While this means that the workforce is now presented with global opportunities, the converse is also true.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workforce now faces greater competition, competing for jobs with counterparts from across the globe.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Building a robust and dynamic workforce and policy system is a multi-year effort.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, implementing an increase in minimum qualifying salaries for work passes can, indeed, result in some work pass holders getting a bump in wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But adjustment to dependency ratios and the longer run signals will help locals get better wages and a higher quality foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we must be careful not to avoid longer-range changes because of shorter-term pains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we debate the cuts, we must be mindful of the strategic imperatives in building a great workforce and the inherent policy tensions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this, Mr Chairman, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask: what is MOM's assessment of whether a points system will be useful in improving the complementarity of the local and foreign workforces?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If, indeed, we are going on this approach, can the Minister share details on the basis of determining complementarity and how the system will be administered?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Is this approach of assessing applications expected to lead to a higher total number of EPs issued and whether could it also lead to a situation where an employer who can find a local hire but choose to hire an EP instead, because the company is able to meet the complementarity and diversity criteria?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Would it go against the spirit of this proposal?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, businesses continue to face a challenging operating environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Operational costs are going up with the upcoming increase in GST, carbon tax and foreign worker levies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Border restrictions have led to some foreign talent leaving the country and not returning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is an urgent need to review our strategies concerning the hiring and retention of foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The competition for talent at the high-end is global.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In 2021, 69% of companies globally reported talent shortages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By 2030, the global talent crunch is estimated to reach 85 million people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This translates into a potential loss of trillions of dollars in economic opportunity for companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Knowledge-intensive industries, like financial services, technology, media and telecommunications and manufacturing are expected to take the hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a framework that gives more certainty to companies for manpower planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the bigger question is, how do we overcome our talent crunch, be very selective and attract the cream of the crop to come here?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we are also extensively upskilling local workers to reduce the skills gap, we should only aim to attract the best from overseas to complement the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we determine what is the best, compared to the mediocre?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we attract the next Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk to contribute their expertise to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What will it take to build the next Amazon, Facebook or Tesla here?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are our strategies to do so, as we come out of COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Amongst talent hiring strategies shared by industry experts, many of them have to do with the hiring process itself and human resource management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Human Resources (HR) Industry Manpower Plan take this into consideration and help our HR practitioners to develop better hiring and talent management practices?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Sir, some have said that certain economic or social sectors are over-reliant on foreign workers, for example, in retail, F&B, construction and healthcare amongst others.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This implies that at least some companies or organisations in these sectors are unwilling to change, slow to adopt technologies and redesign jobs to make them attractive to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When I look at these sectors, I see potential for process and production redesigned to increase productivity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, the delivery of their products and services also encompasses a particular type of work, the type which requires dexterity and eye–hand–leg coordination.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This type of work is difficult to be replaced or designed in a way, not until mobile robotics are advanced and economical enough to be widely deployed.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Most of these jobs may not qualify as complementary because they can, theoretically, be done by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we want better service at retail and F&B shops, more BTO flats, more MRT lines and stations closer to homes and more help to care for our young, our old and the sick.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I understand the objective of tightening access to foreign labour is to drive companies and operators to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, there may be scope for a more differentiated approach.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: So, we roughly know what is an achievable target, what is a stretch target, within a certain timeframe.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: One, jobs that can be significantly reduced through job redesign and use of technology.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Two, the dexterous and eye–hand–leg coordination type of jobs that cannot be easily replaced by automation or process redesign.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad that we are looking at introducing workplace fairness legislation to weed out all forms of discrimination, including nationality discrimination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, I hope MOM can provide an update on the effectiveness of the Fair Consideration Framework; the work of TAFEP and the drive to weed out the triple weak companies; and refinements of the various tripartite standards and guidelines so that we can build upon all these various initiatives and policy measures and further strengthen our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This will allow CPF savings to be tagged to real wage growth, and it is also one way to improve retirement adequacy for Singaporean workers, especially the PMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some elderly residents have insufficient cash to complete the purchase of their 2-room Flexi flats because their CPF Ordinary Account (OA) monies are automatically transferred to the retirement account upon turning 55.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As home loans are not available for Flexi flats, the purchase of a $100,000 flat is often a strain on their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I request that CPF Retirement Account (RA) funds which originated from their OA be allowed to be used for the purchase of 2-room Flexi flats by default as long as the CPF member's RA balance is above the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There should be a simple and clearly stated application process for this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For those whose RA funds for below the BRS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hold CPF can exercise greater flexibility so that elderly residents are not denied a Flexi flat despite large balances in their CPF funds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the payment of the resale levy, can CPF consider allowing applicants who have sufficient funds in their RA or SA to take out an advance from one of these accounts which must be returned with interest within a few years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The applicant could be required to show income documents to prove that they are able to return them amount drawn.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could smoothen the cash flow problem that might be preventing them from completing the purchase of their home, while ensuring they do not prematurely exhaust their retirement funds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will not just elderly flat buyers but also divorcees who have to sell the matrimonial flat and have only half the proceeds to buy a new flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, while CPF has maintained its interest rates at a point where it preserves purchasing power and guards against long-run inflation, the longer time horizons that retirement presents mean that expected increases in longevity and higher retirement income needs should give additional motivation to empower CPF members to enhance their returns when able.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a mere 16% of the over four million total CPF members as of 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There could be many who may wish to see their CPF returns do better than the interest rates offered by CPF but are not confident enough or knowledgeable in the financial markets to buy into the CPFIS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while the world has been moving toward ETFs as an investment product, the available number of ETFs available under the CPFIS is a grand total of six.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many of the global ETFs such as those listed in the US, have total expense ratios which are lower than ETFs and Unit Trusts here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a start, can more passively managed ETFs be made available for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note from my cut last year, then-Minister for Manpower shared that the Ministry had still been studying if a CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) can be introduced to help such members who have the risk appetite and investment horizon but not enough investment knowledge.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the Ministry is updating planning assumptions to strike the right balance between risk and return.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is there a more concrete timetable that can be shared?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should the average Singaporean get access to the diversified investment portfolio of GIC, CPF members could reach retirement adequacy in a way that minimises the risk of short-term market volatility and protect their purchasing power against not just local inflation, but global inflation as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Extending from my Budget debate speech earlier this week, I wish to highlight the need for a Just Transition for the manpower currently within the petrochemicals industry, otherwise known as the energy and chemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With an increasing resistance to working within this space, we may be losing sight of the forest for the trees as we do require petrochemicals, albeit at a reduced level, as we transition to a green economy and society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This does also mean that many in the sector may be at risk of losing their jobs in the near to medium-term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Those who remain in the fossil fuel industry may find some of their jobs fundamentally changed to fit the greening economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many workers in the field should be looking to make mid-career switches into the green economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But how can we integrate a Just Transition in this sector then, so that no one is left behind?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This requires buy-in not just from the Government, but from companies which are invested in the green transition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will such industrial developments in our petrochemical industry affect existing employment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For a start, I hope that both the employers and the Government will work to ensure that as many existing workers as possible can be retrained and converted to new positions under new green ventures within the organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, at this point in time, our aggregate level of green skills level may not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, it is not enough to emphasise on skills and competencies to incorporate into Singapore's education curriculum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our workers in the industry must develop the ability to think at a systems level, to have grit and resilience in order to transit and compete in the global green economy and ready with global talent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I, therefore, ask the Minister for Manpower to give more specifics on transitioning our workers in the fossil fuel industry towards jobs within the green economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will more Continuing Education and Training (CET) courses be jointly developed by NEA together with industry and partner stakeholders and offered by Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), such as Polytechnics and ITEs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will they plan to reach the individuals working within the industry to ensure that they are ready for the transition?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, CPF is our main social safety net.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It can be used for housing, healthcare education and retirement income.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Self-employed persons do not have the benefit of employer CPF contributions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their housing and retirement adequacy are areas of concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UK Supreme Court decided to classify them as workers, a category between employees and self-employed, with some benefits like paid leave and pensions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These gig or platform workers often engage in physically strenuous work with low entry barriers and they also tend to earn less.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, delivery or transportation jobs have a high chance of being replaced by machines with advancements in technology in the not-too-distant future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Researchers in Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) warned of platform workers being caught in a poverty trap.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, I would like to seek further information from MOM: what is the latest number of platform workers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many are unable to meet the basic retirement sum (BRS) now?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who are unable to meet the BRS, what is their average CPF savings?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many have recently completed or are currently attending SkillsFuture courses to upgrade their skills?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to provide two suggestions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The lack of CPF savings is a major concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To encourage platform workers to make voluntary CPF contributions, can MOM consider a special scheme to allow them to voluntarily contribute CPF and withdraw their voluntary contributions on demand?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The income of gig workers is not stable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Due to this volatility, it is important to keep cash on hand.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Gig workers are understandably hesitant about making voluntary CPF contributions over fears that when they need that money, they cannot access it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, however, they have the flexibility to withdraw these contributions when needed, they would be incentivised to contribute CPF to benefit from the higher interest rates offered by CPFB, as salaried employees do.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, can MOM consider making platform companies contribute SDF and use these funds to give extra training support to platform workers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   CPF is our main social safety net.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It can be used for housing, healthcare, education and retirement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CPF inadequacy among platform workers is one area of concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These gig workers or platform workers often engage in manual labour and usually have lower income.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, delivery and transport jobs may be replaced by machines in the near future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to encourage platform workers to make voluntary CPF contributions, will MOM consider a special scheme that allows them to withdraw their voluntary CPF contributions at any time?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they have the flexibility to withdraw their CPF in times of need, they may have less concerns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meanwhile, they will also enjoy higher CPF interest, like other employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second suggestion is for MOM to consider requiring platform companies to contribute to the SDF, so as to provide additional training support to platform workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, last year, I spoke in this House about the importance of FWAs and called upon the Government to lead the adoption of FWAs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In the past two years, COVID-19 has drastically changed the way we work, but as we start to get back on track to living with COVID-19, there is considerable anxiousness and concern that the gains we have made on FWAs could be lost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I am concerned that the signalling from PSD may roll back such efforts in the private sector as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Research shows that FWAs bring various economic benefits, including increased productivity and innovation, better employee morale, as well as attracting more talent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For employees, this can also bring improved work-life balance and mental health.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: To me, the starting point has to be that FWAs are an obligation on the part of employers, and, thereafter, discussions can be made on how these can be tailored to individual job circumstances.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: A related point on FWAs is the idea of a four-day work week.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I shared in a speech last year the benefits that this could bring.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Since then, the UK has also announced a four-day work week pilot.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As shared by the director of the four-day work week campaign in the UK, similar programmes are set to start in the US and Ireland, with more planned for Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Many companies and governments have already started to implement FWAs and four-day work weeks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Finland's Working Hours Act, first passed in 1996, was updated to give employees flexibility to shorten or extend their workday by up to four hours.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Closer to home, local banks, such as UOB and DBS, have also instituted permanent FWAs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Dylan D'Souza was a COVID-19 graduate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was a big deal for the industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, as the economy recovers, human resources are the great challenge ahead.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have time to only touch briefly on three points and I hope you will not buzz me.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One: Singapore being open to global talent is not an option.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are two truths: one, there are simply not enough Singaporeans to do all the jobs that are needed to be done; and two, in fact, our ability to attract the best global talents to work here and complement our local workforce has been a Singapore competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I did speak in Parliament about holding our businesses accountable to Fair Practices in the Workplace (FPW).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hear from the Singapore Human Resource Institute that companies, especially the MNCs, are committed and some have set up a HR compliance unit to ensure FPWs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, fair practices in the workplace should not just be about compliance but an intentional commitment by employers to renew their social compact with their Singapore employees, a key stakeholder.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As for us, the Singapore workers, let us continue to work hard to create value in our roles, to get reskilled to stay relevant, embrace change, think, innovate and adapt and, most of all, act with integrity, responsibility and respect.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We ought to be the difference why companies invest in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My second point: FWAs to attract, retain, diversify and include.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in work from home becoming the norm.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we shift gears to live with COVID-19, it is a great opportunity for companies to rethink the workplace of the future for their workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I think that is not just simply about working from home, but having the choice of flexi-work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With flexibility, I believe that more women, more persons with disability and more seniors can choose to work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My third point: will AI take away jobs?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen many examples from our lived experience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: AI systems should augment work and, in fact, that is actually urgently needed so that the work that needs the human touch, the service quality, the intuition or compassion will have enough people to do them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, trust and understanding are critical and we need as much communication and education in this space, as we need innovation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister give us an update on the progress of the tripartite guidelines being written into law?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister update us if MOM will be advocating and, therefore, supporting companies to move forward with FWAs?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister also update if the Public Service will take the lead and how will the Public Service take the lead to build AI systems to solve part of the manpower challenge?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: He applied for the NUS-ISS Professional Conversion Programme in Full Stack Development and was matched with Works Application Company Limited.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This training enabled Bin Rong to successfully transition into a new profession as a software engineer.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans, we should be proud and heartened to know that our Singapore Budget supports Singaporeans like Dylan and Bin Long, one person at a time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I did not buzz you, but please try to keep your speeches shorter next time, Ms Ang.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: However, one segment of workers where their employability and employment continue to face steep challenges is that of the mid-career jobseekers, those in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: They are most vulnerable to disruptions and restructuring at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: It is a more uphill task for anyone in the middle of their careers to reskill for new jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Hence, we need to intensify support and encourage continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But, of course, there are some who face age discrimination, biasness by their employers and that, we will address it through TAFEP as well as workplace fairness legislation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We already have a range of support measures to help mid-career workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Securing attachments to companies for these mid-career jobseekers can be a good way to help overcome the skills or experience mismatch issues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Also, can I ask the Minister to share the details on the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme which would be enhanced to achieve better outcomes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: To a certain extent, it has helped to encourage employers to retain local staff and expand local hiring.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But this will be a mere stop-gap measure when the JGI ends, if there is no mindset change towards employing seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What other measures are we taking to improve the employment of seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Some of Britain's biggest companies recognise the importance and value of senior workers and had, on their own accord, set targets and plans to increase the number of over-50s they employ by 2022.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The American Association of Retired Persons has an Employment Pledge Programme to recognise companies that are committed to hiring persons aged 50 and above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We must do more to identify the companies that are age-diverse, and work on expanding this group.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, mid-career workers were some of the most affected groups due to the pandemic season.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many experienced loss of jobs and great challenges in being hired over younger workers, despite their wealth of working experience.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some of these mid-career workers are women returning to the workforce after choosing to dedicate their time to the formative years of their children's lives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For these, the pandemic made their re-entry into the workforce more challenging.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: WSG's SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme introduced in 2020 provides many benefits for the mid-career worker.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Apart from learning skills with income supplementation, the attachments and traineeships allow for immersive real-world practice that sets in context their new knowledge.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is particularly valuable for women returning to work in adjusting to the workplace environment that would have changed in their years away from the workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, one key challenge that many of the mid-career individuals face in embarking on this journey is the exploration phase and eventually deciding on the alternative career pathway to choose.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We understand from Executive Career Coaching workshops for PMEs that one of the most important attributes to equip our mid-career workers with is in confidence – confidence for the next phase of their lives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Often, one is unsure of his or her employability in the market, especially if they have only been in one particular role for an extended time.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As such, helping mid-career PMEs understand their transferable skills from past experiences, interests, what energises them will allow them to identify their transferable skills and understand the value they bring to their next role.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This also accords a more holistic assessment of the individual and builds their confidence for the job search.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One career coachee, a tech support specialist for 23 years in the same company, was informed in November 2020 that his company was closing their operations and that he would be retrenched by the following April.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He was turning 50 that year and was the sole breadwinner for his wife and two school-going children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He was very concerned about his employability at the age of 50 and expected not to be employed for a long time after retrenchment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Through the career coaching he received, he was able to discover his skills and recognise areas he could contribute to the current job market and built his LinkedIn profile accordingly.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He was headhunted shortly via LinkedIn as an Automation Engineer and was able to start work immediately after retrenchment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I believe that if we were to invest more time helping our workers discover transferable skills and strengths they have for the current job market prior to the start of their mid-career pathway programme, they will see greater opportunities for selecting a pathway programme that they can flourish in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Over the years, the length of service an employee must serve before qualifying for paid sick leave has been reviewed in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This was in response to an increase in short-term employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Since these legislative amendments, short-term employment contracts have become even more commonplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The percentage of workers on contracts of less than one year has also seen an upward trend.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Many workers find themselves transferred to new employers without even changing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This happens when their previous employer loses a cleaning or building maintenance contract and they are transferred to the new contractor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could increase to four days and 10 days, respectively, after the completion of two months of service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Concurrently, to protect the interests of employers, tax reliefs and public recognition could be extended to employers who implement these more progressive paid sick leave arrangements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This also complements the Government's stance of encouraging workers to isolate themselves and seek medical attention if they feel unwell.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some say Singapore is the most fatigued country in the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Working hard is important, but one cannot work hard without enough rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our minimum annual leave entitlement of seven days is not sufficient for many.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many other countries provide a higher minimum entitlement, including Malaysia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Laos, Qatar, Iran, Japan, South Korea and lots more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many not only have a higher number of minimum days of annual leave, but also provide a higher number of paid public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is hard to see how raising the minimum entitlement will affect employability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Forty-seven percent of employees already get more than 14 days of annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For many businesses which understand the importance of rest, nothing will change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lower-income workers whose jobs are labour-intensive, are likely the ones with the minimum entitlement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is ironic that those who need the most rest have the least rest and also have no access to FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We work hard to increase the salaries of lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should also work hard to increase the time they have to rest.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Every death at the workplace is avoidable and we must do all we can to stop them from happening.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is the Ministry's plan to improve workplace safety for 2022 and beyond?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we move to relax broader safe management measures (SMMs), when can we lift cohorting rules at the worksite, so that workers at construction sites can cross zones and resume helping one another during high-risk work activities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to MOM's data, smaller construction firms – most of them sub-contractors – have a higher workplace fatality rate than bigger contractors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on how many workers have participated in the programme since its launch, and what is the success rate of placing the injured worker back to his workplace?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are there any lessons that we can learn from the programme in the past five years and does the Ministry have any plans to enhance the programme moving forward?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, there remain concerns on whether we are doing enough.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, we need to pay more attention to the mental health of our lower-wage workers, who often find themselves on the stressful frontlines of our whole-of-nation response to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What are the Ministry's plans to improve the physical and mental well-being of our frontline workers, in particular, those in the lower-wage segments?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, research suggests that peer support systems are beneficial for the mental health of employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, every company has a Safe Management Officer (SMO).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us upskill all SMOs to become Work-Life Ambassadors, so that every company will have a representative to look after the work-life harmony of their workers and implement proper peer support systems customised to the individual companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Minister consider changes to the Employment Act to dispense of the need to produce an MC for paid sick leave of up to, say, three to five days out of the 14 days entitlement, being for COVID‐19?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the past few years, fuelled by the COVID-19 pandemic and technological transformations, there have been accelerated changes and developments in our workforce, at work and in the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We had to issue a series of tripartite advisories to keep pace with the curveballs and demands of the new landscape, fuelled by the pandemic and technological developments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: There is an increase in gig economy workers in recent years, but many are in a precarious position.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This is something that the Government has taken note of.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Prime Minister Lee had spoken in his National Day Rally last year on how most gig workers earn only a modest income and they lack protections, such as work injury compensation and, of course, employer CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, there have been arguments made on how, if changes are implemented, markets may be distorted resulting in consumers bearing the costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This may be a false premise, however, as to the extent that the cost burden falls on more relatively better-off consumers who regularly utilise services provided by gig workers, such as food delivery and private hire transport, this could be beneficial from a societal point of view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: After all, the benefits to gig workers discussed should outweigh the costs to relatively better-off consumers of a marginal increase in the price of food delivered to their door by a cyclist on a wet rainy day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Since the UK Supreme Court ruling that Uber drivers should be treated as workers in February 2021, other jurisdictions have moved strongly on gig worker protections.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The EU has proposed a test on how digital platforms manage gig workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Further, with effect from 1 September 2022, all companies which hire foreign workers will be required to pay all their local employees at least the local qualifying salary (LQS).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Gig economy workers today have no control over their earnings and are subject to the ever-tightening incentive schemes in order to barely make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Could efforts be done to ensure that they earn at least a fair wage, with reference to locals working part-time earning at least $9 per hour, as per the LQS?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I am heartened that at this Budget, the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) will be expanded to help more workers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, the payments depend on gig workers making MediSave contributions.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Considering that gig work income may be unpredictable, unstable and, sometimes, insufficient to support their household, they may be discouraged to contribute to MediSave due to more urgent, current needs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, would the Ministry consider relaxing the MediSave requirements on a case-by-case basis to allow the gig workers who are struggling during this period of heightened inflation to benefit from WIS?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In future, though, with no mandatory contributions to CPF, there is a likelihood that their retirement preparations are affected.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, would the Ministry consider mandating or incentivising the gig workers and platform companies to make CPF and MediSave contributions?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Progressive Wage Model (PWM) will also not cover these workers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Career progression with accompanying wage increases will be difficult.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am also concerned about the gig workers if accidents occur.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They may have to pay for their own medical bills while being out of work.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Several platforms provide benefits and protection, in the form of sponsoring skills training courses and providing insurance, though not all.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How can we assist the gig workers pivot to new careers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since the beginning of the pandemic two years ago, concerns over the long-term viability of freelancing in our gig economy have been a major topic of discussion in our society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our increased reliance on multiple segments of this economy, from ride-hailing to food delivery, has shone a spotlight on the plight of this particular group of platform workers – workers who are engaged with major platform companies to provide transport and delivery services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While there are platform workers who take on this job as a secondary source of income to supplement an already decent wage and quality of living, our main concern is for those whose sole source of income is from platform work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These workers resemble employees in a company, yet, due to their present status, are not afforded the protections and perks that employees enjoy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, with limited prospects for wage progression and advancement, the present situation has led to deep concerns being raised over the lack of basic protection for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The matter at hand has been widely discussed in Parliament, and our Labour Movement has recognised these concerns, having taken steps to set up the National Delivery Champions Association in December 2020 and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association in May 2016.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement, indeed, has been pushing for greater protection and representation and welfare benefits that platform workers should be entitled to.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While these efforts have been looked to to push the agenda forward, the Ministry has the ability to engender significant improvements in the prospects and livelihoods of these platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is with this in mind that we seek clarification on the findings and recommendations the Advisory Committee has to better protect the rights of these workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 7 February 2022, MOM's rebuke of prominent blogger Leong Sze Hian's intuitive post last Christmas on job statistics highlighted the issue of job security for Singaporeans once again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do foreign PMETs complement Singaporeans, or do they threaten to take over jobs from Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reality is: it is probably more of a threat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, policy intervention is needed to rebalance the job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This reality, however, is not obvious from MOM's job statistics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The basic problem lies in MOM's reluctance to present the employment data in individual categories of original citizens at the start of the statistical period, new Citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, it has lumped all the figures into one category as locals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we do not have a clear picture of how policies have affected each category of people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And most of the 380,000-job increase would have been because of that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, the composition of the "locals" statistics in 2005 and those in 2020 are different, and most of the job increase is not a real increase.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it truly wants the foreigners to complement the Singaporean Core, then MOM must ensure that the Singaporean jobs are not being threatened.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM should spend its time tackling this problem, rather than wasting time and resources trying to rebut Leong Sze Hian.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, many of us have come across platform workers who are unable to save enough to purchase their own flats, or platform workers who are unwell or isolated and could not earn their daily wages.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: During this pandemic, platform workers who contracted COVID-19 were able to seek assistance from the Courage Fund.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Beyond these one-off assistance schemes, our platform workers need more help to meet their retirement and housing needs and a baseline level of coverage for work injuries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Will MOM be able to provide an update on the discussions of the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How do we ensure that the platform operators are responsible for the well-being of their associates?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leon Perera, if you would like to take your two cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First cut on easing movement restrictions on migrant workers in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What is the Ministry's roadmap to ease restrictions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government explain specific criteria needed for the next round of easing, be it caseload, ICU usage and so on?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Experienced workers might prefer to go home, worsening the manpower shortage and making our economy haemorrhage experienced, more productive workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We are suffering reputational damage in international news.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Al Jazeera quoted one worker as saying: "I feel very sad about the difference in the lives between me and the rest of the people." Chairman, there are practical reasons to ease restrictions, but it is also the decent thing to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, there are economic benefits to retaining migrant workers in our economy who are familiar with Singapore and to increase their productivity, which would mean we need to employ fewer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, a Work Permit holder (WPH) can only transfer to a new job with employers' consent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I support the thrust of this scheme, which is similar to what Workers' Party Members have called for.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it does not go far enough, as it does not apply to all WPHs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I call for it to be extended to all WPHs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In addition, if their existing employer cancels their work permit through no fault of the worker, the worker should be allowed to stay in Singapore for 30 days to enable him to find a new employer, regardless of whether his employer consents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The worker will be responsible for his own food and lodging during this time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He can elect between joining the Retention Scheme, if eligible, or relying on this window.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An article by non-governmental organisation TWC2 states that many workers had their Work Permits cancelled and were repatriated because their employers had no work but did not allow them to transfer jobs, even though other companies needed workers, worsening the manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This proposal will not encourage turnover of workers because it only applies if the employer unilaterally decides to cancel a Work Permit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, to grow productivity and incentivise work pass holders to stay with employers, I propose allowing employers to bond them for up to two years in exchange for sponsoring formal training.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The length of the bond period can depend on the number of training hours, provided that the duration of training and fees meet certain requirements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: ITE could partner BCA, which already runs training courses, to develop appropriate courses to increase our migrant worker productivity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, if you would like to take your two cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Working mothers who breastfeed need support at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: A survey by Singapore's Breastfeeding Mothers' Support Group found that the top reason for stopping breastfeeding was the challenges of expressing milk at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For those still breastfeeding, they reported difficulty in finding time to express their milk at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Sadly, the majority of working mothers surveyed could not express milk as much as they had wanted during work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Laws that guarantee breastfeeding breaks are not new or uncommon.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Countries, such as Indonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia, Japan, India, China, the Philippines, Thailand and South Korea, provide breastfeeding breaks at work or reduction of work hours daily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will MOM support working mothers who breastfeed by legislating to guarantee breastfeeding breaks at work?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, I miss my father very much and I regret not spending enough time with him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I especially regret that I did not take him for his many medical appointments in the year before he passed on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One of these days, you will either say "I wish I had" or "I'm glad I did".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We all need time to spend with our loved ones, especially when they are not feeling well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With an ageing population, many of us will need more time to look after our parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government clearly agrees with this and introduced parent-care leave in the Civil Service more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It really was time we legislate the same leave for all other workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Again, let us not use FWAs to justify not having parent-care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If this reason is true, then why do civil servants with FWAs also have parent-care leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If it is important for civil servants to have both FWAs and parent-care leave, then why not others?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Now, we need to be a family-friendly Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We should introduce parent-care leave for all workers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: That depends on whether Mr Abdul Samad is in the House.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: So, I will take just my first cut first.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: In his speech, Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned that the tighter foreign worker policy is more about calibration.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: He mentioned that it is a calibration to ensure that foreign workers and professionals coming into Singapore are of the right calibre and coming in areas where we really need them, in areas of shortages.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: To ensure its effectiveness, we must also ensure fair employment and hiring practices and also fair treatment at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How are we progressing and legislating TAFEP guidelines to ensure fair employment practices and treatment at the workplace?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Okay, Mr Sharael Taha, next two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The next one will be on advancing the well-being of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Our efforts to uplift low-wage workers have been ongoing for the past decade.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: It is important to ensure that productivity continues to improve, so that wage growth is sustainable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: If real productivity is not achieved, wage growth will drive up costs and make us less competitive in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, businesses also have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we encourage and support more SMEs to transform their businesses, so that low-wage workers can be deployed more productively with more scope for progression?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: This will be further boosted by the Enhanced Workfare Income Supplement scheme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While companies transformed to drive real productivity growth, how do we encourage low-wage workers to continuously upskill and upgrade?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Can we consider a yearly Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) bonus or a tiered supplement scheme, if the worker uses his SkillsFuture credit or attends training or courses yearly to upgrade himself or herself?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In the recent decade, changing dynamics in the workplace and at home have rendered dual-income families greater ubiquity, with many seeking to outsource household duties in order to allow women to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This has meant that Singapore's 1.3 million households are increasingly turning to external help, often in the form of full-time foreign domestic workers, to alleviate domestic responsibilities at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, there still remains a gap in the market for part-time help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This programme allows eligible companies to employ female migrant workers to support part-time cleaning services to households.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This flexibility has allowed families who are unable to afford or provide accommodation in their homes for full-time helpers some access to respite care.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Currently, this arrangement is limited to only providing domestic services to households, such as home cleaning.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Yet, there continues to be a demand for further support in a household's caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our community's social and aged care needs continue to change and have become increasingly intertwined.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We need to allow our seniors to age in place within their homes and their communities, give young mothers peace of mind when they are at work and support family caregivers with respite care alternatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: My resident, Mdm P, who is in her 40s, came to see me teary-eyed and tired and shared that she is the sole caregiver in a family of six people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: She has three children – one of them has a medical condition – two seniors and a husband who is fastidious with cleanliness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The family is unable to afford a full-time helper as they neither have the space for a live-in helper, nor the budget to provide for full board.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: She told me that she would like, from time to time, help in child-minding, assistance in caring for her seniors and support in cleaning her home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In order to have more savings for herself and her family, she takes on food delivery at night after her children have gone to bed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: But we have made strides in augmenting our infrastructural facilities and support systems to advance the caregiving ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Expanding the HSS is a good way to support households that need help with certain aspects of their family but do not wish to hire a live-in foreign domestic worker.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How does the Ministry ensure that there are merits for two distinct schemes and that the policy intent remains for both schemes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In the area of respite care for seniors, will workers be equipped with skillsets to care for the elderly with special needs and challenging conditions, such as dementia?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Will MOM work with MOH to provide training and certification for these workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Additionally, some social service agencies specialising in eldercare as well as nursing homes may already provide such services for elderly caregiving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How does MOM work with MOH and MSF to streamline and harmonise the availability of such services and make it easier for the public to assess their options?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, while calls to improve mental health awareness in the workplace are not new, the issue has taken on an added urgency in the last two years, with the pandemic creating new stressors in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Work-from-home and hybrid work arrangements are at an accelerated pace.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While this has raised work-home flexibility for some households, this also means the lines between work-life and life become increasingly blurred for some and for others, the lack of suitable workspace in their home can take a further toll on the mental health of many employees.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: In some nations, the negative impact of remote working on mental health of employees has led to implementations of new labour laws in Europe.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: From the adjustments to home-based learning in 2020, the stressors our educators in preschool through to Junior College have also evolved over the last two years, with new additional roles, on top of e-learning lesson development.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our teachers took on partial roles as safe management officers, MOH officers and social workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: They are tasked with enforcing evolving safe management measures while finding ways to keep lessons engaging with minimal interaction between students.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: When students started getting COVID-19, teachers were tasked to inform parents of the cases and monitor the Antigen Rapid Test (ART) status of students.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: In addition, with the pandemic's negative impact on the students' well-being, our teachers have also been tasked with needing to check in with students more intentionally and this is despite restricted in-person time allowed outside of class.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Additionally, with teachers also falling ill or being on Health Risk Warning (HRW), they cover each other's duties, thus taking on additional load.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: This is especially significant in our childcare centres.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I know that the well-being of this large population of our workforce would be looked into.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: There is also a need to continue to destigmatise mental illness at the workplace.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While some workplaces offer counselling services as mental health support, many employees do not seek help promptly and hide their illness for fear of being overlooked for a promotion or being treated differently by colleagues.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: The definition of what strong mental health is needs to change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Strong mental health is not about being unaffected by mental strains but knowing when to seek help.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Some employers are concerned that those facing depression and other mental disorders result in lower productivity at work but may not realise that those who are seemingly highly productive can actually be mentally strained.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Productivity should not be viewed as the key indicator of a person's mental wellness and those who seek help with their stressors should not be viewed as weaker than those who do not.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Many of our Singaporean workers want FWAs to continue post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Failure to accommodate would lead to an outflow of talent, especially with Singaporeans being able to work remotely for overseas companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Likewise, foreigners are able to work remotely for companies based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Such cross-border virtual employment can complicate labour laws, CPF obligations and taxation matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What are we doing on this front to ensure that our laws keep up with the trends?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But besides guidelines, we should do more to nudge companies in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Other countries have started implementing new work laws to cater to this trend.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Written contracts for teleworking arrangements, equalising rights for remote and on-site employees and requiring employers to cover remote work expenses are amongst the popular items in remote working legislations around the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Are we learning from other countries and exploring some of these new laws to update our legal framework?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As more companies experience success with this transition, especially when FWA measures allow staff to enjoy better work-life harmony without compromising on productivity, they have been more open to increasing the scale of policies that offer greater work-life balance and flexibility to workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Although COVID-19 is here to stay for the foreseeable future, it is pertinent to ensure that beneficial practices adopted during this time will continue to be enforced.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Given the advantages and demands of FWAs amongst workers, how will the Ministry be encouraging employers to sustain the implementation and expansion of these policies in the long run even after the pandemic has abated?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Beyond making work-life harmony policies a permanent mainstay in the workplace, it is equally important that all aspects of FWAs benefit both employers and employees and remain fair for both parties involved.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This means that employers, on their part, should keep an open mind while employees should exercise responsibility while using FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, potential challenges inevitably remain, such as in monitoring performance with remote working.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In light of this, how will the Ministry ensure that employer appraisals are conducted in a way that is fair to our workers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The prevalence of FWAs and work-life harmony (WLH) policies differs greatly across professions and industries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As we acknowledge the imperative to better WLH measures, how will the Ministry extend FWAs to workers across all sectors of employment, particularly in industries where progress has been slower?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: With the increasing prevalence of FWAs, including work from anywhere and flexible hours during the COVID-19 pandemic, how will MOM encourage employers to sustain these arrangements post-COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we use this opportunity to make our workforce more inclusive and make FWAs a viable option, especially for this group of workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we use this opportunity to realise the latent potential from this group of individuals and encourage more to join the workforce?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Can the Ministry consider promoting FWAs, flexible work hours and work-sharing to create opportunities for this group of individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Can we create second careers for our seniors who are still able to work but do not want to work full-time?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, COVID-19 has changed the way we work, bringing about a paradigm shift in where and how we work.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This shift includes working remotely, flexible working hours and optimising a mix of virtual with face-to-face meetings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we transit into a COVID-19 endemic environment, further changes in work conditions could create stressors to our employees' mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many workers will face the challenge of managing their work-life balance in a hybrid work model, thereby compounding levels of anxiety.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Conversely, these shifts could also present opportunities for better work-life harmony and encourage those who have left the workforce due to caregiving needs to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To tap on the opportunities and mitigate the downsides, there needs to be continuous efforts to support evolving HR practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An important question here is how our tripartite partners continue to support our HR practitioners with progressive practices, which will lead to effective work-life harmony, better mental wellness outcomes for workers, thereby leading to better productivity and better business outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This ensures that there is a standard recognition of good HR practices across the board.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There have been ongoing efforts made in providing FWAs for employees who are non-frontline and in non-shift roles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These efforts, therefore, should be translated to include more frontline and shift workers because such jobs will only increase.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we work towards aligning these common HR practices, I would also like to raise questions on how will MOM encourage employers to sustain this increasing prevalence of FWAs during and post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the areas in the Employment Act that require a review to recognise these changes to work arrangements?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this to work, we need to support our SMEs because, despite much effort over the years, many still lack solid HR policies and capabilities due to resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These SMEs often do not have policies and procedures in place to be able to adapt to new hybrid environments or necessary HR practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As their challenges are real, we need some fresh ideas on equipping these groups of enterprises with forward-thinking HR practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With that, I would like to raise the following questions pertaining to our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What has been the assessment of the Government of all previous efforts to create support services for HR for SMEs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
