text: And if previous efforts to bring SMEs to such services had resulted in a lacklustre response, could there be ideas where our relevant Government agencies design solutions that are brought directly to SMEs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another critical area of our HR policies relates to the foreign workforce component.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore needs a resilient foreign workforce that can withstand future global and regional disruptions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As structural changes continue to take place, MOM could consider how it can further facilitate companies' decision-making on their foreign workforce strategy so that it is more than just complying with set policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How a company determines the best sources for their foreign workforce, in line with the diversity of capabilities required to complement our local expertise, is a strategic choice that cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It impacts how companies will be able to acquire the talent and skills needed to compete and this requires more collaboration with MOM, trade associations and SME management.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The shift in our work environment is real and, therefore, how we work together requires innovative solutions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, if you would like to take your two cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Chairman, the human capital/human resource function is particularly vital, especially as we adapt to the "next normal" of work in the workforce and at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Our human capital/HR professionals play a crucial role in ensuring that every company and business has in place fair, responsible and progressive practices for their workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is so that the majority of these professionals operating in Singapore can be equipped with a rudimentary working knowledge of the norms, standards and practices, including how tripartism works in Singapore as well as how to work with unions and the Labour Movement in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the longer term and in the future of work, some form of accreditation, besides certification, as highlighted by Member Edward Chia, will also be beneficial for this important profession.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As we evolve and adapt to new post-pandemic work norms, good labour-management relations as well as the introduction of more forward-looking and progressive practices, such as PME representation and fair work arrangements, can be valuable factors to consider in awarding the mark.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Members of Parliament and the others who spoke in support of our workers and our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over the past two years of battling COVID-19, our manpower policies had focused on shoring up local employment and keeping foreign workforce policies responsive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We supported businesses in hiring and investing in the skills of a wider pool of jobseekers and helped many jobseekers move into new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through updated work pass requirements, we also ensured local-foreign complementarity and spurred business transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These efforts helped mitigate the impact of COVID-19 and facilitated the recovery of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given the Ukraine war, we are cautiously optimistic that the unemployment rate will fall back to pre-COVID-19 levels in the months ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To capture the opportunities created by a recovering global economy, businesses are starting to increase their hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to provide the necessary support and incentives to restructure our workforce so that we can emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to build an inclusive and comprehensive labour market, where businesses can access the manpower needed for their growth and where continued growth leads to a more equitable and progressive society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The recovering economy provides a better and firmer footing to do so now.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we get this with surgical precision and the right timing – in Chinese, it is 天时地利人和 – Singapore will be a top global city brimming with opportunities for our businesses and our people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first focus is to upgrade the capabilities of locals and the complementarity of foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will strengthen support for locals so that they are equipped with skillsets to take on jobs of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through our foreign workforce policies, we will ensure our businesses have access to the complementary manpower that they need.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For our growth to be sustainable, we must ensure every Singaporean worker benefits from Singapore's growth and no one is left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad will elaborate more in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share our approach to uplifting self-employed persons and strengthening support for mature workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to support our workforce to meet caregiving needs at home, support their mental health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will elaborate more in her speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we will continue with efforts to transform the migrant worker ecosystem to improve their physical, social and mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will be further covered by Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon later on in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will spend the bulk of the speech today elaborating on this segment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned, Senior Ministers of State Koh Poh Koon and Zaqy Mohamad and Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will elaborate further on our other two focus areas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Structural shifts in the economy mean new growth opportunities for our businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As highlighted in the cuts by Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Dennis Tan, some of the shifts include the greening and digitalisation of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The green economy is an area of growth that we are taking very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Minister Gan Kim Yong shared earlier, we have developed a whole-of-Government green economy strategy which looks into the jobs and skills that will be transformed and created as a result of the green transition.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is thus important that our workers are equipped with the necessary skillsets to thrive in this fast-changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Helping our businesses to transform and preparing our workers for the future of work have been longstanding priorities for this Government.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2016, we have rolled out Industry Transformation Maps, or ITMs, for 23 sectors to chart their transformation journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Minister Gan Kim Yong has shared, the Government is working closely with industry stakeholders, unions and academia to update our ITMs to address emerging trends and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In 2021, we announced that Jobs Transformation Maps (JTMs) would be launched to map out the impact of technology and digitalisation on individual jobs over the medium term.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These provide very detailed, job-level insights to help businesses and workers prepare for future jobs and skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To support our scale-up of these programmes, I set up the Jobs Taskforce in September last year to derive strategies to increase the placements of local workers into our key sectors, such as ICT, Manufacturing and Financial Services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, our Career Conversion Programmes, or CCPs, support employers to reskill jobseekers and workers for in-demand job roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They provide targeted support to workers whose job roles might be at greater risk of redundancy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One such individual is Mr Cheng Kim Ann, a 30-year-old who previously worked on aircraft maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He had just completed his Degree in Mechanical Engineering and wanted to seek out opportunities in the aerospace sector when COVID-19 hit.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He re-evaluated his career options and came across a job opening as a manufacturing and equipment engineer with Micron Technology.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To help Mr Cheng assimilate into his role, the company put him on the Career Conversion Programme for the Electronics Sector in November 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: During the three-month programme, Mr Cheng was introduced to the processes in the semiconductor industry which he had to apply in his new job role.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Coupled with the on-the-job training provided by the company, Mr Cheng quickly picked up new skills required for the industry and moved on to learning more advanced skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: During the pandemic, the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and the Jobs Growth Incentive were introduced as extraordinary measures to preserve human capital and expand local hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All these initiatives helped to cushion the impact of COVID-19 on the labour market and provided much-needed relief for the businesses to meet their manpower needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As announced by the Minister for Finance, we will continue to provide support for businesses and worker segments, such as mature workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, moving forward, we will be tailoring our support levels in line with the improved economic and labour market situation and Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate further in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ultimately, support for workers will require a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I urge all of our businesses and all of our employees to support our efforts to help you do better.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Furthermore, the Government will always provide the necessary support for businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But businesses must be willing to set aside time and resources to train up the local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And employees must also be willing to reskill and upskill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The support for businesses under the ITMs is complemented by our foreign workforce policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Foreign workforce policies are key levers to keep our labour market tight and incentivise businesses to transform, move up the value chain and maintain their competitive edge.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Last September, we debated extensively on the issue of foreign manpower in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parliament affirmed the need for Singapore to stay open and connected to the world and for the Government to continue updating its policy levers to secure the well-being and livelihoods of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM has been working steadily on a review of our foreign workforce policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We remain committed to our goals of upgrading our workforce, comprising a strong Singaporean Core and a high-quality and diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: After careful deliberation and extensive consultation with our Tripartite Partners, we are ready to make several important updates to our work pass framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One, to bring in a higher-quality foreign workforce with specialised skills, networks and expertise to complement our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Two, to support employers that invest in reskilling their workers and the transfer of capabilities to build a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Three, to ensure diversity in our foreign workforce, because a truly open and connected labour market must also be able to draw the best from all around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And four, to drive productivity growth, while keeping our reliance on foreign labour at a sustainable level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Above all, these updates will ensure that Singapore can continue to remain open and connected to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As borders start to reopen and labour demand picks up, I want to lay out the roadmap for these changes, which will be phased in gradually.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is to give businesses the certainty they need to plan ahead as they gear up for growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the EP level, we need to bring in highly-skilled foreign professionals, as part of a strong team of locals and foreigners, to grow our economy and to create more good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, we do not set quotas or levies on EPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As announced in the Budget Statement, we will aim to ensure that EP holders are comparable in quality to the top one-third of our local PMET workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To do so, we will set a benchmark for the EP qualifying salary based on the top one-third, or the 65th percentile, of local PMET wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we will revise our EP qualifying salaries based on this benchmark.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given that local PMET wages rise with age, the qualifying salary will also rise with age, to reflect the years of work and experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We know, and we empathise, that the labour market for skilled workers is sufficiently tight.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, this latest move is not intended as a tightening measure.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, it is part of MOM's regular updates to ensure that our qualifying salary keeps pace with local wage growth, so that foreigners are not coming in just because they are cheaper than local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As this is a regular updating of our policy, most EP holders will not be impacted by these changes, because, today, they earn well above the qualifying salary.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are, however, some EP holders who do not meet our quality bar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This group will be impacted, but this is how we constantly ensure that we maintain a high-quality EP stock that complements our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More importantly, we have also set a clear benchmark for the qualifying salary, so that our businesses will have greater transparency, clarity and predictability on how it will be adjusted in future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses should expect regular updating of the qualifying salary to keep pace with local wage trends.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will, of course, consider prevailing economic conditions when making a decision to update the qualifying salary and provide sufficient lead time before each change is effected.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While the qualifying salary is simple to understand and easy to administer, it is also a blunt tool.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are limits to relying solely on it to select complementary foreign talents.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Yip Hon Weng would like to know whether other factors could be taken into account to more holistically assess a candidate's complementarity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The C-O-M-P stands for Complementarity and then the Assessment Framework – COMPASS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is designed to be a transparent system, so that businesses have clarity and predictability for manpower planning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce recommended a points system for EPs last year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Patrick Tay has also raised this earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am glad that there is strong tripartite support for COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members can rest assured that all the details will come later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If I could ask Members to refer to the first page of the handout, under the section "How COMPASS works".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are termed criteria 1 to 4, or C1 to C4.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond these four foundational criteria, we are mindful of two scenarios that warrant special attention.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One, where the candidate possesses skills that our workforce has a shortage of, such as AI developers and cybersecurity specialists.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our locals may have such skills, but we do not have sufficient locals to fulfil the demand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Two, if the firm is undertaking ambitious innovation, hub or internationalisation activities in partnership with the Government, in line with our strategic economic priorities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will work closely with our Tripartite Partners – NTUC and SNEF – and economic agencies to assess industry needs, so that COMPASS is kept current and responsive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: An EP application that "meets expectations" on the four foundational criteria would pass COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the other hand, if an application fares "below expectations" in certain foundational criteria, it needs to make up for it by "exceeding expectations" on other foundational criteria or by scoring bonus points.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: All of the criteria – they are tradeable; none is a veto factor.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Consider a firm in the IT sector that scores "below expectations" on both support for local employment and diversity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It has a low PMET share relative to its industry peers and is bringing in a candidate whose nationality is already over-represented in its firm.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the EP candidate only "meets expectations" on salary and qualifications and is performing a generic job role, the application will not score enough points to pass.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, if the firm is bringing in a candidate in an area where skills shortages exist, the application could make up for it with bonus points.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Alternatively, the firm can hire a candidate from a nationality that improves its diversity and "exceeds expectations" on diversity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In this way, COMPASS incentivises firms with a weaker workforce profile to strengthen their local workforce and diversify, so as not to be disadvantaged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, it still allows them to access highly complementary EPs in areas where skills shortages exist.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, let me be clear – COMPASS is not designed to make it harder for businesses to obtain an EP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A good majority of the applications today would not have issues – this demonstrates that our businesses, in general, are progressive and our policies thus far have brought in complementary EP holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some firms, however, would need to make adjustments under COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And they would know exactly which areas to improve on and how to respond accordingly, given the transparency, clarity and predictability of COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SMEs may be concerned about what COMPASS means for them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Will they be disadvantaged relative to bigger firms?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some may notice that the firm-related attributes under COMPASS are considered as part of MOM's Fair Consideration Framework, or FCF, Watchlist today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: COMPASS builds on our current efforts under the FCF, by applying these considerations upstream, at the point of application.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Businesses will have clarity on what these considerations are.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Once COMPASS is fully rolled out, the FCF Watchlist will be re-purposed to focus on engaging businesses that score poorly on the firm-related attributes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will walk with these firms, to help them to strengthen their workforce profile and to adjust to the new framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay will be reassured that even with the changes to the FCF Watchlist, MOM continues to take fair consideration seriously.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The FCF Job Advertising requirement will continue to apply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers must practise fair consideration in their selection of candidates and MOM will not hesitate to take action against employers who are found to be discriminatory.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also working on plans to enshrine existing fair employment guidelines into workplace fairness legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Coming from the private sector myself, I fully understand and appreciate the importance of transparency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will progressively roll out educational materials and further details on specific criteria.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When COMPASS is in place, employers can use the Pre-Assessment Tool to obtain a "balanced scorecard" of how each application fares prior to submission, so that they know what areas they must improve on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In summary, we have designed COMPASS to be balanced and reasonable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For employers, they will find that the system is responsive to industry's needs and easier to navigate with a transparent, predictable and clear framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It also recognises their efforts to build up a strong local pipeline and maintain a diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For our local workforce, they will have greater confidence that the EP holders here are of high calibre and will better complement their teams, and that their employers will also take efforts to develop their local pipeline and to maintain workforce diversity seriously.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, lastly, for Singapore, COMPASS will allow us to remain open to complementary talent in short supply here so that we can grow our frontier industries to bring us into the next stage of growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai continues to assert that the Government's policy is poor, because its statistics are poor.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the Minister for Finance said in his round-up speech, we get the sense that the persistent requests coming from him for more information are red herrings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They are distractions from the key problem at hand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the 6 July Ministerial Statement, I had already shared that the majority of local PME growth over the last decade went to Singaporeans born in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I repeated this in Parliament in September and stated that this is the same for PMETs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But Mr Leong Mun Wai persists in drawing these divisions, asking for statistics to be split into original citizens, new citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have also alluded, at that particular point in time that, as a society, we should not constantly be drawing such lines.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many of our new citizens and PRs share family ties with Singaporeans, or they had studied, worked, contributed and have lived here for some time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They contribute to our strength as a society and as an economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore is an immigrant nation and openness is one of our society's core strengths that have defined who we are.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I urge Mr Leong Mun Wai – have a care – please do not undermine the cohesiveness we have painstakingly built over the years and please ask people who share your point of view to also have a care for the rest of us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the framework, we think deeply, we consult widely because we know that whatever we do, whatever we implement, will have a significant impact on businesses, locals and Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And once we are confident that our proposals are sensible and implementable, we move.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is why we earlier on rolled out schemes, such as Tech@SG and Tech.Pass, to meet strong demand for skilled workers in the tech sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: COMPASS will buttress these schemes to facilitate access to complementary talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also received feedback from employers who are concerned about bringing in young, high potential employees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are big global firms which have international rotation programmes, where they send both foreign and local employees for overseas postings to gain exposure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are starting with a small group of firms and we will expand the scheme once we have worked out the full details.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the S Pass level, foreign workers perform specialised, technical roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are skilled jobs with good opportunities, which many of our Polytechnic and ITE graduates have an interest in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to continue to ensure that our locals have a level playing field to take up these roles and that S Pass holders are coming in to fill skills gaps and not just because they are cheaper.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also want to spur transformation and job redesign efforts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And this is why we have in place controls for the S Pass, namely qualifying salaries, levies and quotas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As announced, we aim to ensure that S Pass holders are comparable in quality to the top one-third of the local Associate Professionals and Technicians, or APT, workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: How much a firm is willing to pay is a practical indicator of the quality of the S Pass holder.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thus, we will benchmark the cost of hiring an S Pass holder to the top one-third of local APT wages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will raise both the S Pass qualifying salary and levies to reach this benchmark.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is a bigger change, compared to the EP salary criteria.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we will move towards this goal over three steps, to moderate the impact to businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Similar to the EP, the qualifying salary for older S Pass holders will be higher.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thereafter, we will raise the S Pass minimum qualifying salary for new applications in September 2023 and in September 2025.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Each increase will apply to renewals a year later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The exact salary values will be announced closer to implementation date, based on the prevailing local APT wages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just to give a rough sense, based on current local APT wage levels, companies should expect the economy-wide S Pass minimum qualifying salary to be at least $3,150 in September 2023 and to at least $3,300 in September 2025.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As with the EP, the setting of a clear benchmark will give businesses clarity and predictability on how the S Pass qualifying salary and levies will continue to adjust over time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, there have been concerns about the increase in qualifying salaries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Locals have asked if their foreign colleagues will, therefore, automatically get a pay raise, at their expense.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Take a firm that hires 10 employees – nine locals, one S Pass holder.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These employees are all doing the same job, earning the same pay of $2,500.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Will the foreigner immediately get a $500 pay increase, just because of the increase in the qualifying salary?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is about a year and a half from now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I earlier mentioned that this could even stretch out to September 2026, depending on when the S Pass holder is due for renewal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is about four and a half years away at the extreme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The firm will have ample time to think about alternative options, for instance, finding or training up another local.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is especially so if the foreigner is not bringing in enough value to justify the pay increase.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Businesses are, ultimately, profit-driven and they will not just blindly raise costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers have said that it is difficult to find locals in a particularly tight labour market, given the low unemployment rate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But as I had said a few days back, there is still significant untapped supply from both women and seniors outside the workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With our population rapidly ageing, we would want to encourage people to work longer when they are able to and should they choose to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My constant exhortation to everyone is to bring them back into the workforce, encourage them, give them an opportunity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If businesses can do more to redesign jobs to make the jobs more flexible, more inclusive, I think they can attract more of these segments of workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, there are quotas at the S Pass level.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the firm insists on giving the S Pass holder a pay increase without fairly reviewing the pay of its locals, it could find itself in a difficult situation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the locals leave because of the pay discrepancy, the firm may find that it does not have enough quota to retain the S Pass holder at the next renewal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And let us not underestimate the negative impact on productivity of the company when employee morale is poor, or if the company finds itself shorthanded.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We know, on the ground, there will be egregious cases such as these.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In such situations, locals can take their grievances to TAFEP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And TAFEP will engage the firm to conduct a proper salary review, because unfair remuneration practices run counter to the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, you can see, there is a whole thought process that the firm will go through.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If after all of these, the firm still chooses to retain the S Pass holder, it would be because the value that the S Pass holder brings to their operations more than justifies the higher salary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the other hand, suppose we left the S Pass qualifying salary untouched at $2,500.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Yes, the foreigner may not get the pay raise, but our locals' wages will stagnate as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The firm can continue to renew the S Pass holder on the lowest salary required, as long as he is willing to accept it and the firm will then have little reason to raise the pay for the other nine locals who are doing the same job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the Minister for Finance said in his Budget round-up speech, keeping the cost of employing foreign workers low ultimately ends up depressing the wages of local workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some locals tell me that they appreciate the need to raise the cost of hiring S Pass holders but asked us why we could not load it all on levies instead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In that way, the foreigner will not get a pay increase and the Government will get more revenue.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But this is asking us to increase it even more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It does sound like a solution that we can adopt.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Suppose we load all the cost increases onto levies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The levy will have to be much higher than $650.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And these levies will be applied equally to all S Pass holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The more productive firms that hire high-quality S Pass holders well above the qualifying salary will face the same cost increase as less productive firms who are paying just the bare minimum.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Raising levies makes no distinction or differentiation between them – between the productive ones and the less productive ones.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And if all firms have to pay more to the Government, they will have less to pay their workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Will they still have the ability to incentivise their employees to take up new and bigger job roles as they transform?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, there are no perfect solutions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We know that the changes to the S Pass framework are not trivial.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we must do what is difficult now, to build a stronger and more inclusive economy for all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the S Pass moves, businesses that are reliant on low-cost S Pass holders will have to adapt.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They will have to redesign their operations to become more productive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They will have to improve the pay and working conditions for these jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And because of this, they will be in a stronger position to attract locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I understand that SMEs are more constrained in terms of financial resources and many are worried about these moves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have previously spoken about how we will support SMEs through this transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can tap on schemes, such as the Support for Job Redesign under the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG-JR).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To reskill existing employees and new hires to take on redesigned job roles, they can also tap on programmes, such as the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are many of such schemes out there.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SMEs will not have to undertake this transformation journey alone.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the Work Permit level, migrant workers take on important roles which locals are less keen on doing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Yet, COVID-19 has shown us that it is not sustainable to continue to rely heavily on foreign manpower, especially at the semi-skilled level.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Excessive reliance will leave businesses vulnerable to various disruptions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In order for our businesses to survive and thrive, they will need to transform, they will need to increase their productivity and, ultimately, reduce their reliance on Work Permit holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is a reduction from 87.5% to 83.3%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, we will revise the levy structure for both sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To incentivise businesses to adopt more productive technologies, such as Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) and employ more productive workers, levies will be lowered for off-site construction and higher-skilled workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Minister for National Development will share more in his Committee of Supply speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The changes will help support the sectors' transformation and automation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To help defray costs to adopt automation, businesses can tap on grants, such as the Enterprise Development Grant and the Productivity Innovation Project.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The changes to our foreign workforce policies aim to strengthen the complementarity between local and foreign workforce at the EP and S Pass level and to spur industry transformation at the Work Permit level.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I understand that Mr Cheng Hsing Yao and Ms Janet Ang suggested calibrating our foreign workforce policies further to address persistent shortages in certain sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sectors, such as Construction and Process, have higher foreign worker quotas as we recognise that fewer locals join these sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also exercise flexibilities to support essential services like healthcare and the cleaning of public housing estates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Going forward, we will adopt an even more targeted approach by providing flexibilities to businesses that contribute to our economic priorities and in job roles where there are more pressing manpower needs but fewer locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The scheme will provide such firms some flexibility to hire S Pass and Work Permit holders beyond the prevailing DRCs for a limited period of time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For a start, MTI and participating economic agencies will support firms that meet their criteria of undertaking ambitious investment, innovation or internationalisation activities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This would include firms that participate in existing schemes, such as ESG's Scale-up SG and EDB's Research and Innovation Scheme for Companies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition to supporting our strategic economic priorities, we will require these businesses to commit to developing our local workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The details are being worked out and we aim to introduce the scheme later this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, we recognise that some businesses hire rank-and-file workers on S Passes due to the source restrictions for Work Permit holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The list will be introduced on 1 September 2023.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The list will include occupations, such as welders, food processing workers and specialty chefs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I know many enjoy the multicultural cuisines in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that this will reinforce our position as a food paradise, supporting the cultural heritage of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The list will be subject to a quota, amongst other controls, and we will study carefully if more occupations should be added to the list.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, I would like to make it clear that this does not signal a broader liberalisation of Work Permit sources across the board.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Partners have a clear consensus on the importance of uplifting our local lower-wage workers whom the Work Permit holders directly compete with.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we will continue to keep the Work Permit sources tight to support the efforts to uplift lower-wage workers and the ongoing moves to be more manpower-lean.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Taken together, the two schemes, the M-SEP and the NTS Occupation List, will complement the changes we are making to our work pass framework by supporting the growth of businesses that contribute to Singapore's strategic priorities and, ultimately, creating good job opportunities for locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have spoken at length about our upcoming moves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have explained why they are necessary to restructure our workforce to prepare for the opportunities ahead and move towards a more equitable society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many businesses, both local and foreign, whom I have spoken to generally understand this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They have been very supportive and also want to be good, progressive employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One, difficulties in finding workers; and two, increase in business costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the difficulty in finding workers, I earlier touched on the schemes we have to address this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The calibrated reopening of our borders should ease some pressure and, as mentioned earlier, there is still an untapped supply of various segments of our population, and businesses can do more to redesign their jobs to attract these segments of workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On rising business costs, MOM has put in place measures to support our businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes the provision of the Jobs Growth Incentive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also roll out transitional offsets for the increases to senior worker CPF contribution rates and transitional support for the moves to uplift lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The moves are also timed carefully and implemented gradually to moderate the cost and manpower impact on businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, I also want to assure our fellow Singaporean workers that they will always be at the heart of our efforts to drive economic growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also endeavour to create good jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, let me now say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In Mandarin):   This year, we are making various moves to upgrade the capabilities of our local workforce and complementarity of our foreign workforce, uplift vulnerable workers and senior workers, and uphold inclusive and progressive practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Most business owners whom I have spoken to understand the need for these moves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, some employers, more so amongst the SMEs, are concerned.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They share that they face difficulties hiring locals and the announced moves may make it worse.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, they worry about the higher business costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under COMPASS, candidates will be assessed on not just their qualifications and wages but also the hiring firm's diversity and support for local employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For firms with less than 25 PMETs, they will, by default, be treated as having "met expectation" on firm-related attributes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More details of these schemes will be available around the end of this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thirdly, we will continue to support our SMEs in their transformation journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For SMEs looking to automate and transform, they can tap on the Productivity Solutions Grant, the Enterprise Development Grant or the SMEs Go Digital programme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last month, Workforce Singapore launched the new Career Conversion Programme for SME Executives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are just some of the many schemes out there.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I urge SMEs to tap on the schemes available and begin their transformation journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore is a small country, devoid of natural resources.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The road to nation-building has never been smooth-sailing since Independence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Back then, Singapore was often likened to a small fishing boat in a big ocean, which could be easily swept away in a big storm.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our pioneers built on their resilience to ride out the odds and propel Singapore forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: After decades of hard work, Singapore has grown and progressed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are no longer a small fishing boat, but a steady big ship.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope businesses will bear in mind the perseverance of our forefathers and continue to adopt the same attitude in their transformation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Let us create better employment prospects for our workers and work together for a better future!﻿ (In English): Mr Chairman, before I close, allow me to share one aspect of uplifting our workers, which is to strengthen their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As announced in the Budget Statement, we will do so in three ways.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is up from 67% for the cohort that turned 55 in 2021.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, we will implement the next step of the CPF contribution rate increase for senior workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked in his cut about raising the wage ceiling for CPF contributions and Mr Heng Chee How also raised this at the Budget debate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are encouraged by the union's support for the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These efforts are aimed at helping Singaporeans save more and boost their retirement income.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will, however, be meaningless if we do not continue to safeguard the savings that Singaporeans set aside for old age.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is why we must carefully assess any calls for more liberal use of members' CPF monies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In her cut, Ms Sylvia Lim suggested allowing members with CPF balances beyond the required retirement sum to make lumpsum withdrawals from their CPF savings before age 55, highlighting those who face income disruption.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government already provides targeted and directed support to these members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, to help those who face financial hardship during this difficult period, we introduced an entire suite of support measures, including the COVID-19 Recovery Grant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singaporeans will also receive support from existing broad-based permanent schemes, such as Workfare and ComCare.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Importantly, all of these do not draw down on Singaporeans' CPF savings and, as Mr Desmond Choo wisely highlighted, it will not come at the expense of retirement income.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In his cut, Mr Gerald Giam requested for additional flexibility for seniors to use CPF to purchase 2-room Flexi flats and to pay for the resale levy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Before members turn 55, they can request for their Ordinary Account (OA) savings not to be transferred to their Retirement Account (RA) if they intend to use it for housing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: After they turn 55, members committed to a housing purchase may also use their CPF balances in excess of the Basic Retirement Sum to finance the housing purchase.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to reassure Mr Gerald Giam that CPF Board already exercises some flexibility for seniors facing financial hardship seeking to use CPF to purchase a 2-room Flexi flat.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To pay for any resale levy, home buyers can use the proceeds from the sale of their first subsidised flat.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members who still face difficulties affording a property, including 2-room Flexi flats, can approach HDB for assistance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I am sure HDB will also work with relevant agencies like CPF Board to provide help to members based on their specific needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, Mr Louis Chua suggested having members seek higher investment returns on their CPF monies by expanding the range of financial instruments available under the CPF Investment Scheme or allowing members to invest alongside Government investment vehicles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have said this before and, Mr Louis Chua, coming from his financial background, should be familiar that there is no silver bullet in achieving higher returns.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Higher returns come with higher risks and a greater potential for losses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And this is true of any investment fund, and Government investment entities are not immune to this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Desmond Choo pointed out, there is volatility and uncertainty in the investment climate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, CPF members can already invest in a diverse range of products, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), shares and gold products.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The CPF Board welcomes more ETFs to join the CPF Investment Scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, ETF providers' decision to apply for inclusion are, ultimately, based on their own commercial assessment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To safeguard members' interest, the CPF carefully considers these factors, such as investment-related fees and track records of the products, before approving any such applications.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Only products listed under the Singapore Exchange or registered with local authorities are included under the CPF Investment Scheme as foreign products are subject to changing regulations in jurisdictions over which we have no oversight and no control.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More product offerings do not necessarily equate to higher returns.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To ensure that the list continues to remain relevant, the CPF Board will continue to review it on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It strikes a balance between allowing CPF Investment Scheme participants the flexibility to diversify their investment portfolios to enhance their retirement nest eggs, while safeguarding members' interest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is meant for members with the risk appetite and sufficient investment horizon who may not wish to actively manage their investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will provide further information and updates when ready.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Meanwhile, members who prefer not to take any risks with their retirement savings already enjoy interest rates of up to 6% per annum on their CPF savings, where investment risk is entirely borne by the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to look at how we can strengthen retirement adequacy for all of our members, so that they can enjoy financial security in their later years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are making many moves to upgrade the capabilities of locals and complementarity of foreigners, uplift vulnerable workers and mature workers and uphold inclusive and progressive workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we acknowledge there will always be more work to be done.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we will continue relentlessly to put in the hard work of supporting our workers and the businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am sure Members here are familiar with the teach-a-man-to-fish analogy to equip ourselves for the lifelong journey ahead.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, I will continue along the lines of Upgrade, Uplift and Uphold as outlined by the Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will elaborate on how we will upgrade the capabilities of our local workforce, uplift our vulnerable workers, as well as transform our migrant worker ecosystem to support their well-being and resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) were introduced as extraordinary, time-bound measures to preserve human capital and expand local hiring amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The labour market is recovering steadily and unemployment rates continued their downward trend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But we are not completely out of the woods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There are segments of the workforce, such as mature workers that we were more concerned about even before COVID-19 and they have been disproportionately affected by the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Nonetheless, we have made good progress despite the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Among the close to 509,000 local hires supported through the JGI from September 2020 to August 2021, about half were mature workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some mature jobseekers continue to face difficulties in finding permanent jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, we will press on with tackling three structural issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, vulnerable workers who might need additional support in the hiring process; second, mature workers who might need help transiting to new job roles; and third, continuing the outreach to jobseekers requiring career matching services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In all three areas, some of the schemes launched during the pandemic have been especially useful and valuable in supporting the vulnerable jobseeker segments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to keep them in our toolkit of schemes, with some adjustments to their parameters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To address the issue of vulnerable workers who need additional support in the hiring process, we will extend the JGI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As noted by Mr Yip Hon Weng, the JGI has been effective in encouraging employers to expand on local hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It was introduced in September 2020 and has been extended twice since then to March 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Close to 509,000 locals were hired into new jobs by 67,000 businesses from September 2020 to August 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But we will concentrate our resources on the more vulnerable jobseeker segments as I had mentioned earlier, namely, mature workers not in work for at least six months, persons with disabilities and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The JGI will continue to work in concert with other existing structural programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For instance, to support employment of persons with disabilities, we have introduced the Enabling Employment Credit, which Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will elaborate on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together, these schemes ensure that persons with disabilities continue to be well-supported during the economic recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We hope that this will encourage employers to give them a chance, to hire them and train them if needed, so that they can eventually form an integral part of your workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mature workers may also need more help in making career transitions or re-entering employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme, we have equipped workers with skills and opportunities to take on new employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The company attachment programme allows employers to take a greater chance on unproven candidates, provide them with on-the-job training and evaluate their job fit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even trainees who are not offered a job by the host organisation come out of the attachment equipped with skills, experience and industry contacts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Seventy-six percent of trainees who completed or exited their attachments found employment as at October 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some mature workers who may continue to face challenges in finding permanent jobs may already have years of experience and would only require some training to take on their intended roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, we will retain the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme for mature jobseekers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will complement the deeper reskilling provided by our existing Career Conversion Programmes, or CCPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One such mature worker who was willing to undergo further training is Chan Wan Chuen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a 45-year-old back-to-work mother who re-entered the workforce in 2020 after four years, she enrolled in the programme to upskill and improve her employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I am glad to note that her positive mindset had paid off and she has transited well into her role as a Technology Assurance Domain Lead in UOB bank with her newly acquired skills in data analytics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Liang Eng Hwa have asked for more details on how this scheme will be extended.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Janet Ang has called on local workers to keep reskilling and to stay relevant and has highlighted CCPs as a useful way of helping our local workers to do this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The CCPs provide employers with substantial salary support when they hire and train mid-career hires for new job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But this will require both employers and jobseekers to also do their part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I encourage employers to adopt a "plug-train-play" mindset and be prepared to train their new hires instead of expecting a perfect fit from the word go.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The CCP and SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme will support you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I also want to encourage jobseekers to have a more open mind to new possibilities, new opportunities and to acquire new skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To help scale up efforts to reach out to more jobseekers, SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centres were introduced in June 2020 amidst the COVID-19 situation in all of our 24 HDB towns to provide career advisory and coaching services, as well as curate job opportunities available in the vicinity of our jobseekers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To ensure that our job matching services remain readily accessible to our jobseekers in the heartlands, we will maintain SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centres in all 24 HDB towns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Besides having career ambassadors deployed to the centres, we will roll out job kiosks and phone advisory services so that we can flexibly deploy career ambassadors while best meeting the needs of our jobseekers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will also continue working with partners to provide more options for local jobseekers who are mature, long-term unemployed or persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The SGUnited Traineeship programme was introduced amidst a weak labour market to provide fresh graduates with traineeship opportunities to acquire industry-relevant experience and to build up their skillsets and networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the economy recovering, fewer graduates are participating in the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But current trainees will be supported to the end of their traineeships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC shares a close relationship with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They champion workers' interests, as well as trust with employers and the Government to achieve win-win outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Brother Heng Chee How suggested for a tripartite focus to identify priority sectors and occupations for re-skilling, especially for older workers, tapping on NTUC's Company Training Committees (CTCs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As shared by Brother Chee Hong Tat, since April 2019, NTUC has mobilised more than 800 companies to form CTCs and supported companies to develop and implement their transformation plans, including re-skilling of workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has enabled unions and companies to work together to respond with agility during COVID-19, to pivot operations to survive and, at the same time, to help workers sustain livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The efforts of the unions via the CTCs have achieved positive outcomes and MOM wants to accelerate these efforts to benefit more companies and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Sharael Taha has asked for the resources to support NTUC to scale up the CTCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will double the coverage from 250,000 workers today to 500,000 workers in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: About $100 million will be set aside to support NTUC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will invest $28 million to support NTUC to drive this transformation and another $70 million grant to enable companies to operationalise the transformation plans through the CTCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Next, I will talk about our efforts to uplift the different workforce segments, starting with senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As announced during the Budget, the Government will continue to support the retirement adequacy of our seniors by raising the CPF contribution rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By the time we are done with the full increase around 2030, a 55-year-old member currently earning median income can expect his monthly retirement payouts to be boosted by about 10%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government spares no effort to improve the quality and skills of the workforce so that every worker can enjoy better employment prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By 2030, our citizen population aged 65 and above will nearly double to 900,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With an ageing population, it is important to tap on the accumulative human capital of our seniors to keep our economy growing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, employees who are hired at age 55 and above can qualify for reemployment, as long as they have worked for their employer for two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: According to the 2019 recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup of Senior Workers, the Government will start to raise the CPF contribution rate for senior workers from this year and will continue to do so in 2023 to support the retirement adequacy of our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By 2030, a 55-year-old member currently earning median income can expect his monthly retirement payouts to be boosted by 10%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In English): Sir, I will now go on to talk about how we will support self-employed persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For our self-employed persons (SEPs), the Government has progressively strengthened support for this segment of the workforce over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government has worked with insurers to introduce prolonged medical leave insurance, which covers many self-employed drivers and riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management provides mediation services to SEPs to address disputes with their service buyers and SEPs can have their rights enforced at the Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One group of SEPs that we are paying closer attention to are those that work with online matching platforms which provide transport and delivery services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Known as platform workers, they work as private hire car and taxi drivers, or deliver food and goods to our consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government shares the concerns that Mr Louis Chua, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Dr Shahira Abullah, Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Hazel Poa have raised about the welfare and job opportunities for platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Don Wee also highlighted this issue at the Budget debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the emergence of digital platforms, it is now easier for people to source for work on online platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We find that the majority of those who depend on platform work as their main job are older residents aged 50 and above, with non-tertiary qualifications, although delivery workers tend to be younger than other groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform workers have consistently cited flexibility as a reason for taking up platform work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some do it to supplement their main source of income, while others rely on it as their main source of income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Earlier this week, the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) published a study on platform work, involving a survey of more than 900 private-hire car drivers and in-depth interviews with both the drivers as well as delivery riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The study found that the flexibility offered by platform work comes with caveats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For instance, platform workers often have to follow working arrangements and pricing policies set by the platforms, which can change without their consent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some have indicated that they view platform work as a temporary arrangement and would like to transit to regular employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even as we support them in their job search through career matching services and programmes under the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, they may still face challenges, such as lacking the time to job hunt or having the requisite skills to take on new jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a complex issue but, clearly, more needs to be done to close the gap in the protections provided for platform workers to ensure a fairer relationship between the platforms and the platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, we convened an Advisory Committee in September last year that includes representatives from Tripartite Partners to review this carefully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since then, the Committee has been consulting widely through a public consultation exercise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On retirement and housing adequacy, most platform workers expressed concern over their ability to meet both current and future needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Take the example of Ms Peh Xin Xuan, a 28-year-old who has been working as a food delivery rider for many years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For a period, it also served as her main income; it was her full-time job at that point in time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But over time, she found that the irregular earnings, without CPF contributions and the sheer physical demands of platform work took a toll on her financially, physically and mentally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Furthermore, Ms Peh recently applied for a BTO flat with her fiancé.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Like many young Singaporeans, she hopes to use her CPF savings to finance the flat and would like more support to help riders like herself better save up for their long-term needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Failure to do so will result in unmet needs in the future and impose costs on other parts of society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, platform workers already contribute up to 10.5% of their earnings to their MediSave accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To Ms Hazel Poa's suggestion to allow a special scheme that allows platform workers to contribute and withdraw CPF on demand, I do not wish to pre-judge the deliberation of the Committee, but I would like to make a few clarifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is common for returns to be commensurate with the length of holding the funds in the account, such as a fixed deposit account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is impractical to have our cake and eat it by allowing platform workers to withdraw and deposit like a savings account, while still enjoying interest rates higher than what is being offered by a fixed deposit account, for example, in the banks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I would say that the PSP's suggestion is populist but impractical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On financial protection in the event of work injury, platform workers said that they were concerned that injuries would affect their livelihoods, and that the insurance coverage provided was not consistent across different platform companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are heartened by the general consensus among platform companies that they should provide some coverage against work injuries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Committee is exploring how the overall Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) framework can be applied in this setting, but the Committee also recognises that any solution will need to take into account the nature of platform work, including flexibility in working time and the ability to work for more than one platform simultaneously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On the issue of representation, some platform workers said that they lack avenues to voice concerns and expressed the hope that the unions could represent and assist them if there were disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Others wanted a say in contract terms that impact their well-being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are encouraged that, in response, platforms have indicated their willingness to support good industrial relations and improve the working conditions of platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Suggestions from the platforms include the establishment of industry-wide norms through tripartite discussions or with an independent body.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Advisory Committee will be studying these possible solutions, including the idea for unions to represent the platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if the Ministry will be reviewing the Employment Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We do regularly review our legislation, including the Employment Act, in consultation with Tripartite Partners to ensure that they are relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Several major policy reviews are still ongoing, such as in relation to the work of the Advisory Committee for Platform Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is too early to say how the recommendations would be implemented or what legislative changes are needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will consider the recommendations holistically and see how to ensure that our legislative frameworks can support the policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The eventual recommendations will contribute towards a more sustainable equilibrium – one where the costs of labour protections are more equitably distributed and shared across the stakeholders in the platform ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has been a challenging time for everyone, not least for our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They have shown remarkable resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Their health and well-being have been a priority over the past year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
