text: During the last COVID-19 wave in September, migrant workers who tested COVID-19 positive were given timely access to medical support, through regional medical centres, mobile clinical teams and telemedicine consults.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond physical health, we co-created a mental health support ecosystem for migrant workers with our partners, including the Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC) and HealthServe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To date, close to 600 frontline officers have been trained in basic psychological first aid and more than 200 migrant worker peer leaders have undergone self-care and peer support training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They help to detect signs of distress amongst migrant workers more quickly and link them up with counselling services and support helplines in their native languages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As mentioned in my response to the Adjournment Motion put forth by Mr Louis Ng last month and in response to Mr Leon Perera's question on easing of restrictions on migrant workers, let me say that migrant workers can visit any Recreation Centre, or RC, daily since September 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The current community visit quotas are not fully used up and we will be easing in steps the quota and restrictions and as the COVID-19 situation improves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This would provide a return to normalcy for these workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are also prioritising the granting of entry approvals for migrant workers to return to Singapore after they go on their home leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will facilitate them to go on home leave for visits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As we restore economic activities, we will need to continue bringing workers into Singapore safely and help newly-arrived migrant workers settle in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Therefore, in March last year, we started the Migrant Worker Onboarding Centres, which have now been renamed Onboard Centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These function as a one-stop centre for newly-arrived migrant workers, bringing together various entry requirements into an integrated and seamless end-to-end process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers can serve their Stay-Home Notice (SHN) as required, complete a medical examination, and undergo a residential Settling-in Programme (SIP), all under one roof.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Going forward, MOM will continue to improve the well-being of our migrant workers by fortifying housing standards, improving medical support and increasing recreation options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, fortifying housing standards is an ongoing process and is necessary to create a safer and more comfortable living environment for our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As announced last year, the Government will build two new purpose-built dormitories (PBDs) at Kranji and Jalan Tukang.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These dormitories will be built to improved standards to minimise future outbreaks of diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will also work with dormitory operators and other partners to test new and innovative ideas for dormitory living and management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we will support employers in managing healthcare costs while improving medical support for our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will talk about this in the outpatient setting and the inpatient setting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM has appointed four medical service providers to deliver primary healthcare services over six geographical sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This integrated primary healthcare system builds on the medical support plan we set up amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Migrant workers can expect to access a range of primary healthcare services, including acute and chronic care, 24/7 telemedicine services as well as mobile clinical teams, to ensure rapid responses to public health emergencies and concerns in dormitories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The appointed medical service providers will minimise language and cultural barriers in care provision through hiring healthcare workers who can speak the native languages of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This gives employers cost clarity and will meet most of the primary care needs of their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To mitigate the moral hazard of overconsumption and instil personal responsibility, migrant workers will also be required to co-pay a small fee, ranging from $2 for a telemedicine session to $5 for each visit to the medical centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This PCP will be made mandatory for all workers living in the dormitories or working in the construction, marine shipyard and process sectors, as part of work pass requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On the inpatient front, MOM will enhance the coverage of the mandatory medical insurance to better protect employers against large medical bills for their Work Permit and S Pass holders, including those of migrant domestic workers (MDWs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, employers are responsible for the medical expenses of their Work Permit and S Pass holders that are incurred in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Unlike that of locals, the medical bills of migrant workers and migrant domestic workers, or MDWs, are not subsidised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They are also not covered under the national schemes, such as MediShield Life and MediFund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To help employers better manage the medical bills of their migrant workers, employers are required to purchase medical insurance with at least $15,000 coverage for their Work Permit and S Pass holders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As medical costs are expected to increase over the years, more employers may end up incurring larger out-of-pocket expenses on their workers' medical bills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To provide employers greater peace of mind in financing their workers' inpatient and day surgery bills, the coverage of the mandatory medical insurance will be enhanced with the following features.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, we will maintain the first dollar cover of at least $15,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This ensures that the bulk of employers whose workers' medical bills fall under $15,000 continue to be fully protected under the enhanced model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On average, there are over 1,000 employers per year who face bills that are larger than $15,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This ensures that healthcare costs remain affordable and sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under today's existing requirement, if a migrant worker or a migrant domestic worker incurs a $70,000 bill, the insurer will cover the first $15,000 and the employer will be left to bear the remaining $55,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the enhanced medical insurance, the insurer will continue to cover the first $15,000 in full, as per today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This means that the employer pays $13,750, which is significantly lower than the $55,000 he would otherwise need to fork out today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The second enhancement is that we will standardise a list of baseline allowable exclusions across insurers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will provide greater clarity to employers on the coverage that they are entitled to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, insurers may exclude procedures that are not medically necessary, treatments arising from workers' criminal acts or repeat occurrences of undesirable acts by workers such as self-inflicted injuries as well as venereal diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Insurers may also exclude treatments for pre-existing illnesses that occur within the first 12 months of the worker's employment with the same employer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The third enhancement is that insurers will have to offer age-differentiated premiums for workers aged 50 and below and those who are above the age of 50.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will help to keep premiums affordable for the vast majority of employers, given that 95% of our migrant workers and migrant domestic workers are below 50 years old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The fourth enhancement will require insurers to reimburse the claims for inpatient and day surgery bills directly to the hospitals instead of making employers pay for their workers' medical treatment upfront and then claim it from the insurers later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will help employers who are cash-strapped and free up cash flow for businesses and help families who have migrant domestic workers in this process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers with existing Work Permit and S Pass workers will also progressively transition onto the new medical insurance policy when they renew their work passes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The enhanced coverage for medical insurance will be effected for all new work pass applications by the end of 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to thank employers, industry associations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) which have expressed their support for the enhanced medical insurance scheme during our engagements with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The third area we want to do for our migrant workers is to enhance their social well-being and recreational needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our partnerships with NGOs and other whole-of-society partners have been crucial in helping us to support our migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have been working hand-in-hand with our migrant worker community, too, as they would better understand the needs of their fellow workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Rajarathinam Sankaralingam has been a dormitory supervisor since 2012 and assigned to oversee activities in two dormitories.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Koh Poh Koon, my apologies for having to stop you.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As we are approaching 7.30 pm, I would have to invite the Deputy Leader to move the Exempted Business Motion.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, to help sustain the resilience of our workforce, we have put in place measures to drive workforce transformation, to uplift our vulnerable workers as well as transform the migrant worker ecosystem by improving existing healthcare, housing and recreational needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As we continue our work for these groups of workers, there is still much work to be done for others, such as our platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Strengthening our workforce will always be a priority to ensure that we remain resilient in future storms.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to the Non-Traditional Sources (NTS) List, I mentioned that the NTS List will start in 2021.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Deputy Leader, may I invite you to report progress?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This refreshes the Government’s social compact with our lower-wage workers to better support them, provide stronger wage outcomes and for all of us to play a stronger role to create a more inclusive and cohesive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have already made good progress in uplifting our lower-wage workers through efforts such as Workfare and the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In the last five years from 2016 to 2021, we have seen good wage growth across our workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This means that we are reducing the income gap even as we move up as a workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In my speech, Mr Chairman, I will elaborate on the progress of the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers recommendations, and how Progressive Wages and Workfare will continue to be the key thrusts in our efforts to uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I will also elaborate on our efforts to strengthen HR capabilities, so that HR professionals are better able to support businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers report was released in August 2021 and outlines our recommendations for a refreshed approach and ambition for an inclusive and uplifting society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen good progress since the release of the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: New PWM sectors, such as Retail and F&B, have been identified and negotiations are underway.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We can expect to see significant progress in wage outcomes in the coming years for our existing PWMs in the Cleaning, Security, Landscape and Lift and Escalator sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The other existing PWMs have also shown similarly strong momentum, and you can find them in our factsheet; you will see significant increases across the various PWMs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They reflect the Workgroup’s commitment to narrow income dispersion between workers at the lowest 20th percentile and median and this will strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, our overarching principle continues to be that wages and productivity should rise in tandem.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, we not only want wages to rise, but we also want to see productivity increase, through upskilling of workers and through the transformation of businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen more Singaporeans joining sectors with the PWM, such as Security and Landscape, as wages and working conditions improve.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, the employment of locals in the Security sector grew by an average of 5% per year, compared to 2015, which was before PWM was introduced.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is different from some other countries where broad-based minimum wages caused unintended unemployment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is this sustainable progress that gives the Tripartite Partners confidence and the impetus to expand the Progressive Wage Model to cover new sectors and new occupations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This will be followed closely by our second wave of moves in March 2023, just next year about this time, when we implement the Food Services PWM and Occupational Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Given the competitive labour market, we are confident that the PWMs will continue to set the pace for the wage growth of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, even when lower-wage workers who are not covered directly by any PWM should still see good wage growth, as their employers will likely have to adjust their wages to keep pace with the market and to retain them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Beyond uplifting wages, we also want to encourage our employers to pay more attention to other aspects of the well-being of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, following the recommendation of the Tripartite Workgroup, I am pleased to now launch a new Tripartite Standard on Advancing Well-being of Lower-Wage Workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Tripartite Standards (TS) are a set of good employment practices that all employers should implement at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The new Tripartite Standard on Advancing Well-Being of Lower-Wage Workers will encourage employers to provide better workplace support for our lower-wage workers, focusing on areas of training and career development, to provide rest areas as well as care for their mental well-being, as mentioned by Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognise that our workforce has experienced significant disruptions to their jobs during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, it is important that employers cultivate a healthy working environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will elaborate on these efforts in her speech.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To strengthen our social compact, the efforts of the Tripartite Partners and employers alone are not enough.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must recognise that all of us have a role to play – all of us as consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is in this light that the Tripartite Workgroup recommended establishing a new Progressive Wage Mark, or PW Mark, accreditation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to help individual consumers and corporate buyers easily identify progressive employers that are supporting lower-wage workers, and support these employers through their purchases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The PW Mark will be launched in the second half of this year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers that pay at least the relevant Sectoral or Occupational Progressive Wages to eligible workers, as well as the Local Qualifying Salary to all other local workers, will be accredited with the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For employers that have gone one step further to adopt the new Tripartite Standard on Advancing Well-Being of Lower-Wage Workers, they will be recognised with the PW Mark Plus accreditation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To rally the industry to adopt the PW Mark, the Singapore Business Federation has agreed to help administer the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will do our part to lend strong support to the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More details will be announced in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We encourage potential suppliers to apply and obtain the PW Mark early once it is launched.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As we significantly widen the coverage of Progressive Wages and introduce the new Local Qualifying Salary requirement, we recognise that the employers would need some transitional support to adjust to the changes in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government has thus committed its strong support through the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, or PWCS, which was announced by the Minister for Finance earlier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To recap, under the PWCS, there will be two tiers of funding.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With PWCS, the Government is providing direct support to the firms as they adjust to the Progressive Wage and LQS moves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to encourage all firms, including those not in the PWM sectors, to provide wage increases voluntarily in the immediate term when the Government’s support is the strongest.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We urge employers to use this period of support to also accelerate the structural transformation of their business processes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers must take the lead in improving firm-level productivity, so that wage increases will be sustainable for businesses, even when the support ends.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I thus agree with Mr Sharael Taha that employers must press on to innovate and digitalise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is expanding the range of solutions under schemes such as the Productivity Solutions Grant and Advanced Digital Solutions scheme to support such efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Working in tandem with these schemes, I encourage our trade associations and chambers to play a key role in promoting innovation and digitalisation efforts, and share best practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers should also continue to take the initiative in upgrading their skills and applying these skills at work, be it to increase productivity or to take on new roles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This will help them continue to support business transformation and ensure that wage improvements are sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, I fully support Mr Sharael Taha’s suggestions for encouraging lower-wage workers to upskill.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, the Workfare Skills Support scheme provides incentives to encourage lower-wage workers to upskill, through training allowances and a training commitment award.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In 2020, MOM expanded the income qualifying criteria, and increased the amount of allowance and award.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope that our workers will take the opportunity to upskill and improve their career prospects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Moving on to the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme, or what we know as Workfare for short.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare was introduced in 2007 to narrow income inequality; to help our lower-wage workers save more for their retirement; and to encourage our lower-wage workers to work regularly, whether it is for full-time or part-time work, depending on what best suits their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One worker who benefited from Workfare over the years is Mdm Timah Binte Mohamad Kasan.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Being the sole breadwinner while raising two children was not easy for Mdm Timah.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare made it better for her and her family by topping up her income since 2007.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In total, she has received over $34,000 cash and CPF top-ups from Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This has helped her support her husband, who is unable to work and her children while paying off her mortgage for her 3-room HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, she currently receives Silver Support payouts of $720 per quarter.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She also chose to boost her retirement income via the lease buyback scheme and received a $30,000 cash bonus on top of the proceeds from selling part of the flat's lease.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The support from Workfare has not stopped, Workfare will continue to boost her income for as long as she wishes to continue working.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Uplifting our lower-wage workers is a collective responsibility.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As businesses and consumers pay our lower-wage workers better, the Government, too, will do our part.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As announced by the Minister for Finance, the Government will be making significant enhancements to Workfare from 2023.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers will also need to earn at least $500 a month to qualify for Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But allow me to first clarify a statement that I made at the Budget debate about the number of Workfare recipients that would be affected by the new criterion.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The 20,000 figure, as cited by Minister Tan See Leng, had already taken into account the expected wage growth from the PWM expansion and new LQS requirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our objective, in line with Workfare's overall design, is to nudge all our workers, part-time and full-time, towards more gainful employment so that we give them a higher sense of achievement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also want to better target Workfare at those who need it, our lower-wage workers, those with lower household incomes and not casual workers doing vacation jobs, for example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same, we will ensure that those deserving and in need, will continue receiving Workfare, by providing concessions for them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For low-income part-time workers who qualify for ComCare, they will continue receiving Workfare, even if they earn less than $500 per month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are some who want to work more but are unable to do so, due to various personal circumstances, such as persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, PwDs will receive the highest tier of Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope this assures Members of this House that those who are in need and who are deserving of Workfare will continue to receive it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Here, I wish to reiterate a point that Minister Tan also made at the Budget Debate – Workfare is not the endgame for these workers earning less than $500 per month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We need to help these part-time workers find jobs of the appropriate quality and quantity of working hours to earn at least $500 or more if they can.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And we have a whole suite of employment facilitation programmes and initiatives, ready to assist.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare has supported our persons with disabilities (PwDs) for more than a decade and certainly they can do with some extra support.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognise that our younger and middle-aged workers are also dealing with greater family and financial obligations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many of them are taking care of both their children and their elderly parents, while still paying off their housing loan.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is why we will also be increasing Workfare payouts for them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Abdul Samad Abdul Wahab suggested to exclude overtime pay when assessing a worker's eligibility for Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Overtime pay, together with basic pay and bonuses make up a worker's total income that will help support the worker and his or her family.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Workfare helps lower-wage workers by supplementing their income, looking at the total income earned by the worker enables us to better assess the additional support to be provided via Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If we had only used basic salaries to determine who will qualify for Workfare, some workers with low basic salary but high overall pay may displace another worker with higher basic salary but overall, he does not get much more, that is all he gets.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The worker displaced would have needed Workfare more but does not get it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But the worker with high bonuses gets Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, you can see the challenges of why we go towards gross wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, Workfare has supported generations of workers and helped them save more for retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will now extend this same support to younger workers, like Ms Lily.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Lily is an anonymised name as she prefers for us to not use her real name.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Lily is turning 30 years old next year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She bought a flat four years ago and is living with her six children and her elderly mother.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She is current receiving a suite of Government support to help her with her household expenses, including financial support such as the ComCare Short-to-Medium Term Assistance and the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme for her school-going children.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She is looking forward to the boost in income, which will be an additional source of help with her household expenses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She says that the Workfare monies will be used to pay her HDB instalments and buy school supplies for her children.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, these enhancements will apply to all lower-wage employees and self-employed persons (SEPs), regardless of occupation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As pointed out by Dr Shahira Abdullah, to qualify for Workfare, SEPs need to declare their incomes and make the required MediSave contributions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The need to meet CPF obligations is part of Workfare's eligibility criteria and applies to both employees and SEPs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, CPF Board does exercise flexibilities to help SEPs facing difficulties make their CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Progressive Wages and Workfare will continue to form the foundation of the Government's multi-layer support for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Even as we roll up our sleeves and implement these moves over the next two years and beyond, I am reminded of our workers like Mr Mohammed Ali.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In 2017, Mr Ali was an entry-level Security Officer, earning about $1,700 per month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As a worker earning less, he received some support from Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Guided by the PWM's career pathway and with training support from Workfare Skills Support, he upskilled and took on new responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, he is a Senior Security Supervisor overseeing around forty officers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: He earns about $3,100 per month, an increase of $1,400 compared to when he first started.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: He has since graduated from Workfare as his income exceeds the current Workfare qualifying income cap.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While Workfare provided Mr Ali with income and training support when he needed it, Progressive Wages also offered a progression pathway to higher wages and better skills for workers like him.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Ali, I am glad, made the most out of it and I am happy to share that he has graduated from the Workfare scheme, as Progressive Wages has enabled him to earn more.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And by 2028, Senior Security Supervisors like Mr Ali will earn at least $4,430, a significant progress compared to $1,700 when he first started.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Ali’s story is also situated within the larger story of progression for his company, APRO Asian Protection.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Spurred by the PWM and industry transformation efforts, APRO has adopted various tech-based solutions to increase their productivity and their value-add to service buyers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Moving onto a separate but pertinent topic, HR plays a vital role in supporting our workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I thus echo Mr Edward Chia, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Patrick Tay's calls for companies to build up their HR competencies and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Institute for HR Professionals (IHRP) accredits and certifies HR professionals as well as guide their continuous professional development.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To date, there are more than 5,000 certified aspiring and practising HR professionals who support one another developing and sharing HR best practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: IHRP also provides curated learning resources such as HR playbooks as well as facilitates peer-led Communities of Practice and networking opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We encourage more employer and HR professionals to join this expanding network.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM will also continue to work with NTUC, SNEF and the TACs to strongly encourage more HR professionals to be certified by IHRP.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked for an update on the Human Capital Partnership (HCP) programme.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will continue to work with the Tripartite Partners to identify and recognise our progressive employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to recap some of MOM's efforts in Malay.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):   As Minister for Manpower has shared, MOM is committed to shape our manpower policies to enable greater opportunities for all and for us to progress as a vibrant nation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our foreign workforce policies are guided by our goals of a strong Singaporean core, complemented by a high-quality and diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, we will ensure that Employment Pass (EP) and S Pass holders are comparable in quality to the top one-third of our local PMET and APT workforce respectively.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The qualifying salaries and levies will be raised accordingly to meet this benchmark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also introduce Complementarity Assessment Framework, or COMPASS, as part of the Employment Pass framework.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: COMPASS is a points-based system that holistically evaluates the complementarity of EP applicants.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It will take into account; firstly, salaries of applicants relative to local PMET wages in their sector; second, the applicant’s qualification; third, the firm's nationality diversity; and fourth, the firms support for local employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also look at other factors like whether the candidate possesses skills that are in shortage or whether the firm supports our strategic economic priorities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In future, EP applicants must meet the EP qualifying salary, and also score sufficient points under COMPASS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Existing EP holders must also meet these criteria when their work passes come up for renewal.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So what does all these mean for our local workforce?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: COMPASS will take into account many more factors in the assessment of EP applications.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with the requirement for a higher EP qualifying salary, locals can be assured that EP holders here are of good calibre, and not just because their salaries are lower than locals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With COMPASS, locals should also feel more assured that firms will be incentivised to improve their employee diversity and strengthen their support for local employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, we will also build on our existing efforts to uplift lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will expand the PWM and implement a new Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) requirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is doing its part, through the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) which funds the wage increases of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also enhance the Workfare Income Supplement scheme, to provide higher payouts to all our Workfare recipients.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, to conclude, our suite of measures will benefit both lower-wage workers and businesses, and allow us to renew and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And this reflects this Government's, the PAP Government's strong belief and commitment to uplift our lower-wage workers and to build a fair and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our social compact must be one which everyone enjoys the fruits of growth and that no worker is left behind as Singapore progresses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must be careful to not let our social compact be eroded by inequality, otherwise our society, including our businesses, will not function well and much less thrive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have made significant progress over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And Mr Chairman, we will do even better in this decade in creating a more progressive and inclusive society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair, Mr Desmond Choo, for painting very clearly the challenges that businesses and workers are going through and that are lying ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our workplaces have seen major changes amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In these unprecedented times, we have had to adapt and be flexible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Working from home, which was not so common pre-COVID-19, became the default mode of work for many of us for the past two years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As our workers navigate uncertainty and stresses during this period, the importance of supporting their well-being has come into even sharper focus.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: My speech will focus on how the MOM team will uphold inclusive and progressive workplace practices, so that everyone has fair opportunities to contribute and thrive at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As we prepare to celebrate International Women’s Day tomorrow, we should take pride in the resilience of the female workforce in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While there is progress made, there is room for more women to be active in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I participated in the nation-wide Conversations on Singapore Women’s Development last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A key concern raised amongst women was the need to help caregivers remain in or re-enter the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We recognise that women carry heavier caregiving responsibilities at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To manage the caregiving roles, some women work part-time with reduced pay or even leave their careers early.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I agree with Ms Janet Ang and Ms Yeo Wan Ling that one of the ways to enable more women to continue their careers is having access to flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This can be in the form of flexi-time, flexi-place, or flexi-load.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Flexi-work arrangements apply to men too and allow more balanced sharing of caregiving responsibilities between women and men.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The pandemic has underscored how flexible work arrangements can strengthen business continuity and resilience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As pointed out by Mr Yip Hon Weng, flexible work arrangements help companies better attract and retain talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Flexible work arrangements also allow businesses to tap on a larger pool of workers including seniors and differently-abled workers, as suggested by Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We applaud the many employers who have made the shift towards flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some have shown their commitment by adopting the Tripartite Standard on flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Adopters are recognised as progressive employers that put in place HR practices for effective communication and implementation of flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Public Service has taken the lead by adopting the Tripartite Standard and I urge more companies to come on board.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I agree with Mr Edward Chia, Ms Janet Ang, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Yip Hon Weng, that we have made much progress in flexible work arrangements in the last two years and we must not lose momentum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Similar to the trend in other parts of the world, flexible work arrangements will become the norm of future workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will work with our Tripartite Partners to see how we can sustain flexible work arrangements, even as the safe management measures are relaxed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For countries, such as the UK and Australia with legislation that provide employees and caregivers the right to request for flexible work arrangements, employers can still reject the request on business grounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To create real change on the ground in the next few years, our priority is to help employers overcome barriers in implementing and continuing flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For some, the nature of business operations makes it challenging to offer flexible work arrangements and they lack the know-how to overcome these barriers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These concerns and hesitations are understandable, as different sectors will have different needs and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Louis Ng have raised, work from home is not as practical for frontline work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers could consider other forms of flexible work arrangements, like flexi-shift scheduling, staggered work hours and job sharing, which offer workers alternative flexibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) has started training HR professionals to implement hybrid work and after-hours communication policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Separately, the Institute for HR Professionals (IHRP) has developed a playbook on hybrid workplaces to help employers and HR professionals implement hybrid work, as well as update their HR processes, fair appraisal of employees on flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is important to build mutual understanding and trust between employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: That is why instead of taking a legislative approach for various workplace practices such as flexible work arrangements, after-hours communication, mandatory breastfeeding breaks, we first focus on equipping employers to find the right balance between supporting employees needs and business needs. "Take care of your employees and they will take care of your business" – these wise words are from Mr Richard Branson, founder of the Virgin group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I believe many employers here feel the same way too and will support employees' requests, if they are reasonable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, employees need to demonstrate that progressive workplace practices help to improve staff morale, productivity and loyalty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Those who feel aggrieved and are not able to address their grievances within their companies, may approach TAFEP for assistance and advice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Members have also asked for further review of leave provisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On Mr Louis Chua's suggestion on a four-day work week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Members may wish to refer to the TAFEP website for information on how companies can implement such flexible work arrangements, including policy templates on four-day work week and case studies of companies that have successfully done so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And Mr Louis Chua perhaps may want to consider implementing four-day work week in his company or department too and share the useful insights with the rest of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On the issue of sick leave for employees on short-term contracts, we encourage employers to exercise flexibility in granting medical leave before the three-month mark.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To attract manpower in a tight labour market, it is in the interest of employers to be flexible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar suggested that we do away with the need for employees to produce a medical certificate in order to take sick leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nonetheless, the Employment Act does not prohibit employers from providing sick leave without MC and companies are free to do so as part of their talent attraction and retention strategies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Tripartite Partners agreed that employees should not request MCs from workers who test positive for COVID-19, so as to alleviate the stress on healthcare workers and avoid compromising the standard of care of other patients who genuinely require medical care during this period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Given our ageing population, challenges faced by our workforce in meeting caregiving needs of elderly family members will increase.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked how we could better support household's needs for domestic services, including caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In 2017, MOM introduced the commercial Household Services Scheme (HSS) which allows HSS companies to hire more migrant workers to provide part-time home cleaning services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: HSS workers are deployed to multiple households on a part-time basis to provide selected households services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This gives households, especially those that need domestic help for only a few hours a day or a week, more options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Households will be able to engage services of HSS companies to look after their children at home or provide some basic assistance for their family members in activities of daily living.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about the safeguards that the Government will put in place to ensure HSS workers are qualified to provide child-and-elder-minding services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, there are already private companies that provide such services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will study the industry best practices as we expand the scope of HSS companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In Mandarin):   To give households more options to meet their needs for domestic services, the HSS allows eligible companies offering domestic services to hire more migrant workers to provide part-time home cleaning services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Given the growing caregiving needs due to our ageing population, and to better help parents to balance their work and family commitments, we are looking to broaden the HSS scope to allow participating companies to provide the basic child-minding and elder-minding services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Households will be able to engage HSS workers to look after their children at home or provide some basic assistance for the elderly in activities of daily living.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We aim to implement the HSS expansion in the second half of this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In English): I will now touch on our efforts to enhance mental health and well-being of our workforce, an issue that Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Melvin Yong had raised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Last year, the Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Council expanded the code of practice on WSH Risk Management (RMCP) to explicitly cover mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The expansion included examples on how employers can identify, evaluate and manage risk related to mental health at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This marks a significant step in recognising that workplace safety and health includes mental well-being, beyond physical injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is also an Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) playbook on "Workplace Mental Well-Being” to guide HR professionals to support their colleagues as well as mental well-being talks and workshops by the WSH Council and the Health Promotion Board that employees can attend at little or no cost.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We still have some way to go ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government will step up our support to help organisations become more progressive in adopting mental well-being initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are studying how Employee Assistance Programmes, which provide confidential counselling services to employees, can be made more accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As raised by several Members of the House, there is growing demand for support for workers with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: According to a recent Singapore mental health study, one in seven people in Singapore had experienced a mental health condition in their lifetime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to strengthen employment support for persons with mental health conditions so that they are not excluded from employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Persons with mental health conditions may need flexibility in their work schedules to continue with therapy or counselling while remaining in employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For those who had to leave their previous jobs or even take an extended break from the workforce, they may need help with the job search process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Agencies, including the Institute of Mental Health, Singapore Association for Mental Health and Singapore Anglican Community Services, provide pre- and in-employment support to persons with mental health conditions and their employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Dawn is one of the individuals who has benefited from the support provided by the Singapore Anglican Community Services (SACS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Dawn’s bipolar condition started in her teens and she received counselling during her times in the University.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A year into her job, she suffered a relapse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She found out about SACS’ Integrated Employment Services programme where she enrolled for training in conflict resolution, stress management and personal effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With support from SACS’ job-matching services, Dawn successfully gained employment in a full-time job and she has since remained in employment for more than two years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Dawn’s story is a positive example of how some persons with mental health conditions manage to receive the right support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we worry that some may not be referred to available employment support and some employers, through lack of awareness about mental health support and conditions, wrongly believe that it is too difficult for them to support employees like Dawn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will study the effectiveness of the pilot and develop further plans to support employees with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will also work with other members of the Interagency Taskforce on Mental Health and Well-Being to strengthen the ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will be engaging stakeholders and members of the public to get their views.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The pandemic has not stopped our efforts to foster fair workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This move will help to manage longer-term anxieties over ageism and provide better protection for vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A wider range of penalties can also be imposed on errant employers, commensurate with their wrongdoing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To this end, we must put in place a robust system to deal with claims, while keeping it efficient for workers and employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness is deliberating these important matters and continuing to consult widely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The committee will report on its recommendations in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To conclude, the COVID-19 pandemic has brought about many challenges and given rise to new stresses at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, it has created opportunities and stronger impetus for us to push ahead for changes to make workplaces fairer and more inclusive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In his speech, Minister Tan See Leng spoke about sailing our ship into an even brighter future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The MOM team will do our best to support employers and employees as they chart the path towards more progressive workplaces where everyone can thrive in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Together, we can sail our ship sustainably for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, I have two clarifications for the Minister for surfacing COMPASS as a framework to improve foreign worker complementarity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How does it work hand-in-hand with the Fair Consideration Framework to prevent abuse for companies hiring workers above that pay range?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second clarification: how can the HR community also play a role in supporting capability transfers and localisation efforts?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to thank the Member Mr Desmond Choo for checking with us on the $20,000 bar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The EP holders at the $20,000 mark are typically senior management.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They include C-suite personnel and specialists at the top of their field.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is especially so in certain sectors, including even some of the SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They would most likely have gone through even more selective hiring processes to be appointed in their company since these roles typically require very specific capabilities or skillsets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Regardless of these exemptions, firms are expected to practise fair hiring and also to develop their own local talent pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More importantly, our focus is to continue to help Singaporeans rise to the top by enabling them to compete strongly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As an aside, we actually look at the number that would cover local PMETs and we find that this is the level at this particular point in time, that COMPASS would cover quite a high majority of individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, the bar, at this point in time, is at $20,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In terms of the HR community playing a role in supporting capability transfer and localisation efforts, we work closely with the community, whether it is Singapore Human Resources Institute (SHRI) and IHRP, and beyond that, with companies, trade chambers and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We exhort them to encourage HR managers to undergo courses to continue to keep themselves updated with regard to our policies and the improvements towards our framework, whether it is the Fair Consideration Framework to now, the new COMPASS that we are going to roll out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we believe that for those companies that have a very progressive and forward-looking vision in terms of improving their workforce, we will not hesitate to roll out schemes to support them to transform because, at the end of the day, our focus is raising the quality of the EP holder, to the top one-third in the local PMET space.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Of course, we believe that, with that, we will be able to uplift our entire workforce to compete globally and also not just develop and grow our own timber, but to be complemented by foreign talent in those areas that we have a need for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One, will the transparency of the COMPASS framework allow employers to game the new system and, two, would the new COMPASS framework allow for more EP holders into Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps I can answer the Member's second question first.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The fact that the majority of our existing EP holders pass COMPASS is an encouraging one.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It instils the discipline on such firms to continue to select complementary candidates, uphold diversity and also support local employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, COMPASS is an added framework on top of the first stage, which is the EP qualifying salary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are and there will be some firms which do not pass COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These include firms that make a habit out of hiring EP holders not due to their high calibre or skills but based on the convenience of networks, such as an old boys' club, and without taking heed of our calls to develop the workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: COMPASS ensures that these firms cannot simply carry on with their status quo and they must fundamentally relook their hiring practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will have in place strong governance measures to guard against any dishonest attempts to game COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, we already have processes to enforce against fraud for criteria considered in our current framework, such as salary and qualifications.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Similarly, we will also develop processes around additional criteria, such as the shortage occupation list.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the necessary verification processes upon which we look at the educational qualifications criterion will also be put in place.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, of course, employers certainly will not be able to get away with changing the job title to claim bonus points.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have spent many, many weeks and months deliberating this framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Two of the criteria which concerns the firms are, I believe, a couple of firsts that we have achieved as a nation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My exhortation to all employers is to support us, strengthen and work with us collectively, as a country, as an economy, as a nation, to build this complementarity and to build our local workforce to compete globally.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we have embarked on a fairly seamless process in terms of data analytics and we will be able to pinpoint and triangulate this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, under the new COMPASS framework, what constitutes top-tier institution and at what level and if qualification needs to be relevant to the job that is going to be performed?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And the second clarification is, besides qualifications, does MOM evaluate the quality of these candidates to determine if they are, indeed, high-quality talents that complement our local workforce?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Other factors such as relevant working experience are more subjective and are more difficult to assess at-scale.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The description of the top-tier universities as available on the MOM's website.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They do not just involve and include universities, they also include top-tier technical and vocational institutions as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A firm can still hire a candidate with no degree-equivalent qualifications if they perform well on other criteria.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, under COMPASS, there is greater flexibility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have said earlier on, there are vocational institutions which are highly recognised in specific fields that can be included in the list of top-tier institutions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is regarding the own account workers' welfare cut that I filed on the gig economy workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just wanted to ask if efforts can be done to ensure that they at least earn a fair wage in terms of reference to locals working part-time earning at least $9.00 per hour as per the LQS, given that these workers are not really in control in terms of their earnings power and are subject to all these incentives?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to the cut on the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The reason being if you look at where the global markets have been since August 2016 when the recommendations were put forth, they have been up 67%, so this delay does have real cost and opportunity cost to our members in terms of their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The whole definition of a gig worker is that they have the flexibility to work as many hours as they want, whenever they want and with whichever platform they want.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is very hard for us to then decide what would be the minimum wage that they can earn if they do not clock certain minimum number of hours.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is the flexibility that is inherent in the nature of the work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We must recognise that it is difficult for us to set that.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The market, of course, can decide at some point but in our work looking at the platform workers, we are specifically working at three areas, which are the housing and retirement adequacy, basic workplace protection against injuries, and some of these payment-related algorithms or wage-related outcomes could well be left to the third part of the work, which is on representation by either a body of platform workers; or the unions as a voice for the workers to seek better compensation and remuneration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, may I answer Mr Louis Chua's second point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I think that when it is ready, we certainly will come back and update everyone in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I further ask Minister, under this framework, if the employer were to meet all the requirements under COMPASS, is MOM obliged to give the EPs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And if that is the case, will that lead to a situation where the total number EPs issued would be even higher than before?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is to Senior Minister of State Koh.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am really happy that Senior Minister of State is going to continue the Skills and Future Centre at the 24 HDB hubs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have one in Bukit Panjang and the residents are really grateful for the convenience and advisory provided there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Senior Minister of State whether would the centre go further to beef up capabilities to do more local job-matching and with the intent to bring back or facilitate stay-at-home mothers or the seniors to rejoin the workforce?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our design of COMPASS is, as it has arisen as an acronym, the "C-O-M-P" part stands for "complementarity" and the "A-S-S" stands for "assessment".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For us, the complementarity is what is most important.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are trying to make this framework a very highly differentiated system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A set of criteria which allows us to titrate, to be able to right site and continually uplift our level of competitiveness vis-a-vis globally.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our aspiration is to be a global city, brimming with opportunities for our Singaporean Core, continue to provide opportunities for our young.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we are also cognisant of the fact that with the multiple disruptions, the pace of the disruptions, the accelerated change and transformation that is happening around the world, it behoves us to now move into a system where every EP holder coming, every foreigner coming in, will have to pull his weight in working, complementing our locals, at the same time supporting and driving our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As long as the economy continues to grow, as long as it continues to uplift all of our Singaporean Core in terms of their skillsets, their competencies and, most importantly, their take-home wages, I think the framework will be one which is going to help us to continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As long as the general economy and industry can accept and be able to stomach, we will continue to improve this framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that the Member can take away that this is a very highly differentiated framework that we are trying to achieve for all of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are actually forward-deployed nodes, to be more embedded in the heartlands to allow easier access by many of our heartlanders who are jobseekers as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In that sense, the main career centres curate all the jobs that are available, including those on the MyCareersFuture portal but, at the same time, as the main centre looks at the jobs that are put onto the market, they do curate them according to the vicinity of each of the forward-deployed centres and push out these job lists to the centres as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For jobseekers who are probably within one of the nearer centres when they look for jobs, the centres can also recommend jobs that are closer to where the jobseeker stays so that it helps to facilitate some of these part-time work, or for people who may have mobility issues who want to work closer to home.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I want to assure Mr Liang Eng Hwa that this is already being done today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the shortage occupation list factor in both occupation and industry?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, we may have a shortage of software developers in general, but not necessarily software developers in the financial services industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if such a distinction by industry is not made, MOM might be making it easier for companies like banks to hire foreigners without necessarily improving the opportunities for talented Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, does the Minister expect that the outcomes in terms of the foreign-local talent mix in companies to remain largely unchanged, moving forward?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the national diversity attribute of COMPASS, can I understand if MOM sees some concentration risk in having too high a percentage of any one foreign nationality in a firm?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think to his first point in terms of whether COMPASS was from the FCF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The fact that the vast majority of the companies actually passed when we put them through the COMPASS framework is actually a testimony to the fact that many companies for the past many years have been very progressive, very responsive and very nimble to the needs of our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As far as the diversity itself is concerned, it is a function also of the ability of the company to access the skill sets based on the individual sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, let me put it across in a perhaps, in a more illustrative way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those that are in IT, particularly when you deal with a lot of cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and very advanced deep machine learning, even with deep-tech itself, depending on the sources where this group of skill sets are developed, you are not able to completely assume that you are able to get these skill sets from all around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we designed it to be such that in those areas that we have shortage of, and the fact that when we decided to pivot into the Industry 4.0 roadmap, we therefore needed to complement these gaps.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, when we took all these into account, we felt that this is what is needed for our economy to get to the next step.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The exact details, going into the granularity of why we want to do the cut-off at the various benchmarks, I think I have already explained it before in my speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that sort of gives the Member some insights into the thinking behind it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My third point was asking about the national diversity criteria inside COMPASS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Is it because MOM sees certain concentration risks in having too many people, too many employees from one nationality in the organisation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: If not, what is the reason for including that?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To a certain extent, it is also guided by the current pandemic that is still ongoing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When certain restrictions came about, we were not able to let this group of EP holders travel freely back to their home countries to visit their relatives and come back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, taking all of these into consideration, taking into account our various needs, we came up with a very nuanced approach in terms of the framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, there are many foreign media articles out there that claim that we have become extremely unattractive because of the fact that many of these EP holders could not come back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And actually, it is not because of the fact that we did not allow them to come back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It was just because of public health border controls that we were not able to bring them back here to work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, with that, this framework, to a certain extent, was also influenced by that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On his question on the remaining 6% of lower-wage workers not covered, what their profiles are like.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think more than half are earning $1,400 and above, even though they are not covered by progressive wage moves, they are already earning that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But the question would more be, what are the exclusions and why did we exclude this group.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But really, if you look at most minimum wage systems around the world, there are exclusions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Well, in our estates, I think we probably know many of them, mom-and-pop shops who employ their own family members sometimes to help them out and one way we could do is to support in our Progressive Wage Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope that in Aljunied and Sengkang, you can also encourage many of these merchants, mom-and-pop shops to come on board the Progressive Wage Mark and say yes, please support and pay our workers more, and we will be happy to give you the Progressive Wage Mark if they do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, to that extent, rest assured, for this set of workers, they will still get Workfare and other benefits, whether it is Silver Support and so forth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Back to your question, what are their profiles, they are typically your micro-SMEs in the heartlands and typically family businesses too.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I thank Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad for sharing regarding the Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: My understanding of the $2,500 is actually basic salary plus allowances.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, maybe it is my first time, or just maybe it is my ignorance, that it has to include bonuses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: That means, every year, that worker cannot be earning more than $30,000.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If he or she earns more than $30,000 annually, hence he or she does not qualify for the Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Why I ask to exclude overtime pay, I believe the Government and us as a society want to help those low-income, right?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: So these low-wage workers, why do they actually need to do the extra overtime work to actually supplement the cost of living daily?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope while today the Government, as Senior Minister of State has explained, that they have to include, moving forward, can we really explore?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Because someone that needs to do overtime, he wants to earn that extra income to meet the cost of living and also he is spending time away from his family.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do we actually want to take that into consideration by excluding overtime pay?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In my speech earlier, I did explain why we do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you look at Workfare, we push it slightly above that to cater for wage growth in the coming years and what we hope is to continue supporting lower-wage workers at that level.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
